title: Spark Debugging & Performance Skill Check
tagline: Triage and evidence, Spark UI and log forensics, executor memory and the four distinct OOMs, GC, data skew, shuffle and AQE, join strategy and cardinality, driver bottlenecks, UDF cost, file layout, the three partitionings, caching, cluster sizing, stragglers, and cost per TB. Diagnosis before configuration.

questions.prompt: A pipeline that normally finishes in 40 minutes has been running for three hours. What is the correct FIRST action?
options: Split the elapsed time into scheduler time and Spark execution time
Add more executors to speed up the remaining work
Enable adaptive query execution
Increase executor memory and restart the job
questions.explanation: A 'three-hour pipeline' may be a 40-minute Spark job sitting behind a two-hour upstream sensor wait plus cluster provisioning. The orchestrator knows queue time, retries and provisioning time; the Spark UI does not. Splitting the clock first tells you whether this is a Spark problem at all — and prevents you from tuning a segment that is only part of the total.

questions.prompt: Your job is RUNNING but slow. Which single comparison most efficiently separates the major cause families?
options: Total shuffle bytes versus total input bytes
Max task duration versus median task duration, cross-referenced against task input size
Executor count versus the number of partitions
GC time versus wall-clock time
questions.explanation: Max-vs-median duration separates 'one thing is slow' from 'everything is slow'. Cross-referencing against task INPUT then splits the first case again: if the slow task also read far more data, it is skew; if it read a normal amount, it is a straggler or an unhealthy host. Those three outcomes — skew, under-partitioning, straggler — have almost no fixes in common, so getting this wrong wastes the whole incident.

questions.prompt: A pipeline fails and there is no application ID, no driver log and nothing in the History Server. What does this tell you?
options: The event log was disabled, so evidence was lost
The driver ran out of memory before it could register
The failure is upstream of Spark — orchestration, provisioning, permissions or packaging
The cluster manager killed the application immediately
questions.explanation: No application ID means Spark never started. The failure lives in the scheduler, cluster provisioning, IAM/credentials, dependency or JAR resolution, the Python environment, or driver initialisation code that runs before the session is created. Nothing you know about shuffle partitions is relevant, and the Spark UI does not exist to be consulted. A suspiciously round total duration (60s, 300s, 900s) is a strong tell for a provisioning or auth timeout.

questions.prompt: A job COMPLETED successfully but took 126 minutes instead of its usual 42. What technique actually works here?
options: Enable speculative execution to eliminate stragglers
Profile the driver's CPU usage
Re-run it with more executors and compare
Compare against a baseline metric by metric, looking for the one that moved disproportionately to input
questions.explanation: Nothing crashed and the output is correct, so there is no dramatic evidence to follow. The only reliable technique is baseline comparison across a fixed set of counters — input bytes, output rows, shuffle read/write, spill, GC, task count, task p50/p95/max, executor-hours. The metric that moved OUT OF PROPORTION to input is the diagnosis. If you have no historical metrics, the first deliverable from the incident is the instrumentation, not the fix.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes how Spark incidents propagate through the stack?
options: Incidents typically have a primary origin layer but cascade upward, so the visible symptom is often several layers above the cause
Incidents are non-deterministic and cannot be reliably attributed to a layer
Each incident is confined to exactly one layer, which is why you must identify that layer first
Incidents start at the top and propagate downward into the data layer
questions.explanation: A real incident commonly cascades: a skewed key (data) creates an oversized partition (tasks), which spills (memory), which saturates local disk, which lengthens GC, which misses a heartbeat, which loses an executor, which triggers a FetchFailedException. You meet it at the BOTTOM of that chain. Every fix applied downstream of the origin buys time and nothing else — the discipline is to walk back up to the layer where the cost actually originates.

questions.prompt: Before changing ANY configuration during an incident, which of these should you capture? (Select all that apply.)
options: The application ID
Current runtime versus the historical median for the same weekday
Input bytes and the slowest stage's task p50/p95/max
The exact wording of the alert message
The active Spark configuration from the Environment tab
questions.explanation: Application ID, runtime-versus-baseline, input volume, slowest-stage task quantiles and the effective configuration are all needed to prove afterwards that a change helped. The alert's wording is not evidence — it is the notification that evidence is needed. Without a baseline captured BEFORE the change, any improvement is unattributable.

questions.prompt: You change five Spark configs at once and the job gets 30% faster. What is the most serious problem with this?
options: The improvement might be within normal run-to-run variance
You cannot attribute the gain, some changes may have hurt, and a config chosen without a mechanism will not survive a change in the data
Five changes will make the job harder to roll back
Other engineers will not be able to reproduce the result
questions.explanation: All four are downsides, but the deepest is the third clause. Attribution failure means you carry unexplained settings forever; masking means the real available gain may have been larger; and — worst — a fix chosen without naming a mechanism breaks the moment the data shifts. If you raised memory when the real cause was skew, it works until the hot key grows 20%, and the runbook then says 'increase memory' because that is what worked last time.

questions.prompt: Describe the disciplined debugging loop for a slow Spark job, and explain why 'change a config and re-run' fails as a method.
questions.model_answer: The loop is: SYMPTOM (what the alert said) -> EVIDENCE (UI, logs, metrics) -> BOTTLENECK (which level, which stage) -> ROOT CAUSE (the mechanism, named) -> FIX (one variable) -> VALIDATE (measure, compare, keep or revert) -> DOCUMENT -> add a regression detector. The key properties are: a falsifiable hypothesis that names a mechanism rather than a resource; exactly one variable changed; a prediction of which metric should move and roughly how much; and confirmation of the MECHANISM (spill went to zero, max/median fell, shuffle bytes dropped) rather than runtime alone, because runtime can improve for unrelated reasons. 'Change a config and re-run' fails because it produces no knowledge that transfers: you cannot say which change mattered, you cannot safely revert, and you cannot tell the next engineer why the setting exists. It is also slow in practice — each speculative re-run on a large job costs real wall-clock time and real money, and the folklore loop (slow job -> more memory -> retry -> pray) never terminates because it never identifies a cause.
questions.explanation: The senior signal is naming the mechanism and the confirming metric, plus acknowledging Spark's real run-to-run variance — a small delta from a single pair of runs is usually noise.

questions.prompt: In the Spark UI, which tab is authoritative for what configuration your job ACTUALLY ran with?
options: The Jobs tab
The Executors tab
The Environment tab
The SQL / DataFrame tab
questions.explanation: The Environment tab (or /api/v1/applications/<id>/environment) lists the effective configuration for that run. It outranks the Apache documentation, your platform's documentation and anyone's memory — managed platforms routinely override defaults. Check it before arguing about what a default is, and check it again after someone says they 'didn't change anything'.

questions.prompt: A stage's summary metrics show median task duration 26s, max 34 minutes, and the average is 26.4s. What is the correct reading?
options: The median is misleading because it ignores the tail
The stage needs more executors to reduce the average
The average shows the stage is healthy; the max is an outlier to ignore
The average is irrelevant — stage wall clock is set by the LAST task to finish, so the max explains the runtime
questions.explanation: With 5,000 tasks at 26s and one at 34 minutes, the average is ~26.4s while the stage takes 34 minutes. The average is not wrong — it is irrelevant. Read MEDIAN to size the normal unit of work, MAX to explain the runtime, and the RATIO between them to name the cause. Adding executors changes nothing when 4,999 slots are already idle waiting on one task.

questions.prompt: Which Spark UI metric most directly indicates that partitions do not fit in the memory available per task?
options: Spill (memory) and Spill (disk)
Shuffle Read Blocked Time
GC Time
Scheduler Delay
questions.explanation: Spill is data evicted from execution memory and written out — it appears only when something actually had to be paid for. It is the most actionable pressure signal, and should be read alongside Peak Execution Memory (how close you are to spilling) and the executor peak-memory columns. GC time indicates allocation pressure, scheduler delay indicates placement/queueing, and blocked time indicates fetch or network waits — different problems.

questions.prompt: High 'Shuffle Read Blocked Time' across essentially ALL tasks in a stage points to what?
options: Data skew on the join key
Tasks waiting on remote shuffle blocks — network, remote executor pressure, or oversized blocks
Insufficient executor memory
An expensive Python UDF
questions.explanation: Blocked time is time spent waiting for shuffle blocks to arrive. When it is high for one or two tasks it can accompany skew; when it is high across the board it points at the transport layer — network saturation, an overloaded external shuffle service, or blocks so large that transfers stall. The tell is low CPU with the job still crawling: you are waiting, not computing.

questions.prompt: Which UI observation most strongly suggests the DRIVER is the bottleneck rather than the executors?
options: Shuffle write greatly exceeds input bytes
Every task in the dominant stage is slow and uniform
Long gaps in the Jobs timeline with no active stage, plus active tasks far below total slots
GC time is a large fraction of task time on several executors
questions.explanation: Gaps with no active stage mean the driver is doing something serial — file listing, plan compilation, or the write commit. Combined with idle slots, that says work is not reaching the executors. Other driver tells: hundreds or thousands of tiny jobs in the Jobs tab (a loop submitting an action per iteration), and task counts in the millions, where per-task metadata alone becomes a driver heap and CPU problem. Adding executors makes this WORSE, because it gives the same driver more tasks to track.

questions.prompt: In a scan node of the SQL tab, an empty `PartitionFilters` list on a partitioned table means what?
options: The filter was pushed all the way into the file format
Adaptive query execution removed the filter as redundant
The table has no partitions defined
Directory-level partition pruning is not being applied, so the scan is reading far more than it needs
questions.explanation: Populated `PartitionFilters` is how you confirm directory pruning happened. Empty, with input bytes equal to the whole table, means the predicate is being evaluated after reading rather than used to choose directories — commonly because the partition column was wrapped in a function or compared against a mismatched type. Verify rather than assume: also read the 'number of partitions read' metric.

questions.prompt: Why can a physical plan printed by `EXPLAIN` differ from what actually ran?
options: With AQE enabled, the plan is re-optimised at runtime using real shuffle statistics, so joins may convert and partitions may coalesce or split
EXPLAIN randomises join order for cost estimation
The physical plan is only finalised after the first action completes on the driver
EXPLAIN always shows the logical plan, never the physical one
questions.explanation: Adaptive Query Execution (on by default from Spark 3.2.0) re-plans stage by stage using measured sizes: a sort-merge join can be promoted to a broadcast join, partitions can be coalesced, and eligible skewed partitions can be split. A static EXPLAIN is therefore a proposal. The SQL tab of the finished run shows the plan that actually executed, including AQE nodes — that is the only authoritative view.

questions.prompt: Which physical-plan operators should immediately raise suspicion when you did not expect them? (Select all that apply.)
options: CartesianProduct
BroadcastNestedLoopJoin
SortMergeJoin on two large tables joined by an equality condition
BatchEvalPython sitting between two fused regions
ReusedExchange
questions.explanation: CartesianProduct and BroadcastNestedLoopJoin mean no usable equality condition survived — comparisons scale with the product of the inputs, so these are alarms rather than information. BatchEvalPython marks a row-at-a-time Python UDF boundary, which both costs per-row serialization and blocks the optimizer from pushing filters through. SortMergeJoin on a large equi-join is the correct, robust choice. ReusedExchange is GOOD news — a shuffle computed once and reused.

questions.prompt: Which REST API call gives you a stage's task-duration percentiles without reading the UI?
options: /api/v1/applications/<id>/executors
/api/v1/applications/<id>/stages/<stage>/<attempt>/taskSummary?quantiles=...
/api/v1/applications/<id>/jobs
/api/v1/applications/<id>/environment
questions.explanation: `taskSummary` with a `quantiles` parameter returns the same summary metrics the UI renders, as JSON — including duration, shuffle read and spill at each quantile. This is how you build baselines and automated skew detection (tracking max ÷ p50 per run) instead of eyeballing screenshots during an incident.

questions.prompt: Task locality is mostly `ANY` on a cluster reading from cloud object storage. What should you conclude?
options: Dynamic allocation is releasing executors too aggressively
Placement has failed and should be tuned
Essentially nothing — there is no local replica to schedule near on object storage, so ANY is expected
The executors are under-provisioned
questions.explanation: Data locality is an HDFS-era concept: it matters when a block has a physical home on a specific node. On object storage there is no 'local' copy, so ANY locality is normal and is not a finding. On an HDFS-style cluster, mostly-ANY locality IS worth investigating.

questions.prompt: You open a slow stage. Describe, in order, the specific metrics you read and what each one rules in or out.
questions.model_answer: 1) Duration at p50 and max, and the max/median ratio — separates 'one thing slow' from 'everything slow'. 2) Shuffle Read (and Input) size at p50 and max — this is the discriminator: if the slow task also read far more data, it is skew; if it read a normal amount, it is a straggler or an unhealthy host. 3) Spill (memory) and Spill (disk) — any meaningful spill says partitions exceed the execution memory each task actually gets, which is roughly (heap x memory.fraction) / cores. 4) GC Time as a fraction of task time — a rising fraction over the stage points at an accumulating live set (caching, aggregation state) rather than the data. 5) Shuffle Read Blocked Time — high across all tasks means transport, not compute. 6) Scheduler Delay — high means placement or a driver too busy to dispatch. 7) The executor id / host column for the slowest tasks — if several share one executor, it is a bad node, not the data. 8) CPU time versus duration — CPU ~= duration with no spill and no blocked time means an expensive per-row operation such as a UDF, regex or JSON parse.
questions.explanation: The senior signal is treating shuffle-read distribution as the discriminator rather than stopping at duration, and grouping slow tasks by executor before concluding skew.

questions.prompt: `org.apache.spark.SparkException: Job aborted due to stage failure` appears in the driver log. What is this message worth?
options: It indicates a driver memory problem
It means the stage exceeded spark.stage.maxConsecutiveAttempts
It identifies the root cause precisely
Almost nothing on its own — it is the outermost wrapper; the cause is further down the Caused by chain, often on another host
questions.explanation: The exception you are shown is almost never the exception that happened. Read from the bottom and keep descending the `Caused by:` chain until a message names a RESOURCE (heap, container limit, disk, a file, a credential) or a VALUE (a column, a cast, a row). If the chain bottoms out in a Spark internal such as FetchFailed or ExecutorLost, the real cause is on a different executor — get the host from the message and read that executor's own log.

questions.prompt: An executor disappears. Its log ends mid-line with no exception, and the container exit code is 137. What happened?
options: The process was killed from outside for exceeding the container memory limit — nothing threw
The network partitioned and the driver declared it dead
The executor was gracefully decommissioned during a scale-down
A Java heap OutOfMemoryError was thrown and swallowed
questions.explanation: Exit 137 is the classic memory-kill signature: the cluster manager or kernel killed the whole process because the CONTAINER exceeded its limit. The JVM heap may have been half empty — what overflowed is outside it (Python workers, native libraries, direct buffers, off-heap). Nothing threw, which is why the log simply stops. Exit 143 (SIGTERM) instead usually means decommissioning or preemption.

questions.prompt: How do you distinguish a Java heap OOM from a container memory kill, and why does it matter?
options: They are the same failure with different names
A heap OOM throws a stack trace and the task retries; a container kill leaves no exception and the process vanishes — and raising executor.memory makes the second one WORSE
A heap OOM only affects the driver; a container kill only affects executors
A container kill can be fixed by raising spark.task.maxFailures
questions.explanation: They have opposite fixes. A heap OOM means one task's working set exceeded its share of the heap — the answer is usually less data per task (more partitions, fix skew) or fewer cores per executor. A container kill means total container memory was exceeded, usually by NON-heap consumers; raising spark.executor.memory inside a fixed-size container grows the heap and squeezes the very region that overflowed.

questions.prompt: A `FetchFailedException` appears. What does it most often actually mean?
options: The driver ran out of memory tracking shuffle metadata
The network is unreliable and retries should be increased
The executor that held those shuffle blocks died, so the cause is on another host
The shuffle partition count is too low
questions.explanation: Fetch failures are usually a CONSEQUENCE. Shuffle output is not replicated — it lives on the local disk of the executor that produced it — so when that executor dies, the data is gone and Spark must re-run the map stage that produced it. Raising retries cannot resurrect a dead executor; it converts a fast failure into a slow one and destroys the evidence. Find the EARLIEST executor death and read its own log.

questions.prompt: A job runs for four hours (normally 50 minutes) with repeated stage attempts and hundreds of fetch failures, then fails. What is the correct investigative focus?
options: The total number of fetch failures as a measure of network health
The stage with the highest shuffle write
The last failure before the job aborted
The FIRST executor death — everything after it is cascade
questions.explanation: This is a retry storm. Each executor loss destroys its map output, forcing re-execution, which puts the same pressure on the same cluster and kills another executor. Sort the Executors tab by removal time, take the earliest death, and read that executor's log and exit code. Raising spark.stage.maxConsecutiveAttempts only makes the storm last longer and cost more before failing.

questions.prompt: `ERROR HeartbeatReceiver: Removing executor 23 with no recent heartbeats`. What is the most common underlying cause?
options: A long stop-the-world GC pause on that executor, or CPU starvation
The driver ran out of file descriptors
The executor finished all its tasks and idled out
A genuine network partition
questions.explanation: The executor is often perfectly alive but unable to answer. Check that executor's GC time as a fraction of its run time first, then host CPU and disk. Raising spark.network.timeout (Apache default 120s) is the 'larger waiting room' fix — it makes you slower to notice the patient is sick. It is occasionally justified on a genuinely high-latency network, but never as step one.

questions.prompt: `Task not serializable`, caused by `NotSerializableException: com.acme.DbConnection`. What is the fix?
options: Mark every class in the project Serializable
Capture only what the closure needs — pull values into locals, or construct the object inside the task via mapPartitions
Increase spark.kryoserializer.buffer.max
Switch spark.serializer to Kryo
questions.explanation: The closure captured something that cannot cross the wire — commonly `this`, because an instance field was referenced from inside a lambda. Copy the needed value to a local variable first, or build the non-serializable resource on the executor, typically once per partition with mapPartitions. Making everything Serializable is a workaround that ships objects you never wanted to send.

questions.prompt: `WARN TaskSetManager: Stage 3 contains a task of very large size (18234 KiB)`. What is happening?
options: The result returned to the driver is too large
The partition is too large and should be split
Data is being shipped inside the task closure — broadcast it or read it on the executor instead
The shuffle block size limit was exceeded
questions.explanation: A large task means you captured data in the closure — a big lookup map, a config blob, a collected list. It also inflates 'Task Deserialization Time' in stage metrics, which is how you spot it from the UI. The fix is to broadcast the lookup once, or read it from storage on the executor.

questions.prompt: A PySpark job fails with `Python worker exited unexpectedly (crashed)` caused by an `EOFException`. What does the EOFException tell you?
options: The Arrow serialization format was mismatched
The worker exceeded spark.driver.maxResultSize
The input file was truncated
Only that the pipe to the Python process closed — it is never the root cause
questions.explanation: The JVM-side EOFException just reports that the worker went away. Look in the same executor's stderr for what actually happened: a Python traceback (a crash on a specific record), a segfault line (a native library fault), or NOTHING at all plus a container-kill event (the worker was killed for memory). Those three have different fixes.

questions.prompt: A job succeeds for 55 minutes then fails with a permissions error. What does the TIMING suggest?
options: A credential or token that expired mid-run — the fix is in credential refresh, not the policy
The output path was deleted by another job
The cluster lost its instance profile
A misconfigured IAM role or bucket policy
questions.explanation: Two shapes mean opposite things. Failure AT THE START is a misconfiguration — wrong role, wrong path, wrong policy. Failure late in a long run is almost always an expired credential, and the tell is that the same job succeeds whenever it happens to run faster. Fix how credentials are refreshed rather than broadening permissions.

questions.prompt: `ExecutorLostFailure` is reported. Which of these are genuine candidate causes? (Select all that apply.)
options: A Java heap OOM inside that executor
Container or pod kill for exceeding a memory limit
Spot / preemptible instance reclamation
Local disk failure or the scratch volume filling
A skewed join key in the query
questions.explanation: 'An executor disappeared' is all the message says, and at least seven things produce it: heap OOM, container kill, Kubernetes eviction, YARN preemption, node failure or spot reclamation, network partition, disk failure or disk-full, and graceful decommissioning. A skewed key is not itself a cause of executor loss — though skew can lead to spill, which fills disk, which CAN kill an executor. That is a cascade, and the distinction matters when you decide what to fix.

questions.prompt: What does `spark.executor.memory` actually control?
options: The total memory of the executor container
The JVM heap of each executor — one region inside the container, not the container itself
The memory available to execution and storage combined
The per-task memory budget
questions.explanation: The container also holds JVM non-heap (metaspace, thread stacks, code cache, direct buffers), Python worker processes, native library memory, optional off-heap memory, and miscellaneous overhead. Several of the most common failures happen in the regions spark.executor.memory does NOT describe — which is why raising it is not a general-purpose remedy.

questions.prompt: With `spark.memory.fraction` at its Apache default of 0.6, what does the remaining share of usable heap serve?
options: The JVM's reserved off-heap region
Cached blocks only
User memory — your objects, UDF state, closures and Spark's own internal structures
The shuffle write buffers
questions.explanation: Unified memory (execution + storage) gets 0.6 of usable heap by default; the rest is user memory. This is why raising memory.fraction is a late knob rather than an early one: it takes room from the region that holds your materialised objects, so with object-heavy code you can convert a spill (recoverable, slow) into an OOM (fatal).

questions.prompt: An executor has a 16 GB heap and 5 cores. Roughly how much unified memory does each concurrent task get, and why does it matter?
options: 16 GB / 16, based on the default partition count
It depends only on spark.memory.storageFraction
16 GB — memory is not divided between tasks
Roughly (usable heap x memory.fraction) / 5, so a few GB — which is why HALVING cores doubles per-task memory at no extra cost
questions.explanation: Unified memory is per EXECUTOR, shared by its concurrent tasks. Per-task memory is approximately (heap x memory.fraction) / cores. That makes spark.executor.cores one of the most underrated knobs in Spark: lowering it raises per-task memory for free, and in PySpark it also reduces the number of simultaneous Python worker processes per container. The counter-pressure is more JVMs, each with its own overhead and its own copy of every broadcast.

questions.prompt: Executors are being OOM-killed in a PySpark job, but heap dumps show the JVM heap only ~40% used. What is the leading hypothesis?
options: Python worker processes — one per concurrent task, living entirely outside the JVM heap — pushing the container over its limit
spark.memory.fraction is set too low
The driver is broadcasting too much data
A memory leak in Spark's shuffle manager
questions.explanation: In PySpark there is one worker process per concurrent task, so an 8-core executor can run 8 Python processes each holding whatever the UDF materialises. That memory is outside the heap and counts against the container. The cheapest fix is usually reducing spark.executor.cores — fewer simultaneous workers AND more JVM memory per remaining task. Then make the budget explicit with spark.executor.pyspark.memory, and only then raise overhead plus the container size together.

questions.prompt: When is raising `spark.executor.memoryOverhead` the right response?
options: Whenever an OutOfMemoryError is thrown
When the container was killed with a healthy heap and non-heap use is genuinely large — and you raise the container size with it
Whenever tasks spill to disk
When the driver exceeds maxResultSize
questions.explanation: Overhead covers what lives outside the heap. It is the right knob for container kills with a half-empty heap. Two cautions: on some managers overhead comes out of the same total budget, so raising it without raising the container size just shrinks the heap; and if the underlying growth is unbounded (a Python worker holding whole partitions), raising overhead only delays the next failure.

questions.prompt: Which of these is the LEAST likely to help an executor heap OOM caused by data skew?
options: Filtering out sentinel and NULL keys that cannot match
Isolating hot keys into a separate branch
Doubling spark.executor.memory
Salting the aggregation and combining in two stages
questions.explanation: Under skew, one partition is orders of magnitude larger than the rest. Doubling memory buys one doubling of headroom against a partition that may be 100x the median — it will fail again as soon as the hot key grows. The durable fixes change the DISTRIBUTION: remove keys that cannot match, isolate hot keys, salt with a two-stage combine, or redesign the model. Memory is the correct answer only when the per-task working set is genuinely irreducible.

questions.prompt: What does `spark.memory.storageFraction` (Apache default 0.5) actually guarantee?
options: The fraction of the container reserved for off-heap storage
The proportion of shuffle data held in memory before spilling
A hard cap on cache memory
A floor of unified memory that cached blocks are guaranteed to keep — not a hard split
questions.explanation: Execution and storage borrow from each other within unified memory. Execution can evict cached blocks; storage cannot evict execution. storageFraction only sets the floor storage is guaranteed to retain. This asymmetry is why caching in a job that is already short of execution memory tends to make things worse.

questions.prompt: `spark.memory.offHeap.enabled=true` is set with a size, but the container size is unchanged. What is the likely outcome?
options: Container kills — off-heap memory now competes for the same container budget, so effective memory shrank
No change; off-heap is drawn from the OS page cache
Faster shuffles due to reduced serialization
Longer GC pauses
questions.explanation: Off-heap execution memory is a legitimate technique for large execution memory without heap-scan pause cost — but it lives inside the container like everything else. Enabling it without enlarging the container reduces what is actually available and produces exactly the container-kill failure it was meant to avoid.

questions.prompt: `Total size of serialized results ... is bigger than spark.driver.maxResultSize`. What is the appropriate first response?
options: Set spark.driver.maxResultSize to 0 (unlimited)
Stop returning that much to the driver — write to storage, aggregate first, or sample
Raise spark.driver.memory to match
Increase the number of shuffle partitions
questions.explanation: The guard (Apache default 1g) exists to fail your job cleanly instead of killing the driver. Raising it is occasionally right when you have deliberately decided the driver should hold that much and have sized driver memory for the DESERIALIZED form, which is typically several times the serialized bytes. Setting it to 0 removes the airbag.

questions.prompt: Which fixes are usually better than 'increase executor memory' for an executor heap OOM? (Select all that apply.)
options: Increase the number of partitions so each task holds less
Reduce spark.executor.cores to raise per-task memory
Remove or isolate a skewed key
Unpersist a cache that is pinning the heap
Increase spark.network.timeout
questions.explanation: More partitions, fewer cores per executor, removing skew and unpersisting a cache all reduce the working set a single task must hold, or free heap that was deliberately occupied. Network timeout has nothing to do with memory — it changes how long the driver waits before declaring an unresponsive executor dead, which at best hides a symptom. Note that more memory can also make a job LESS stable: bigger heaps mean longer stop-the-world pauses, which cause heartbeat timeouts, which cause executor loss, which causes fetch failures.

questions.prompt: Which four distinct failures are commonly all called 'OOM', and why does naming them matter?
options: Driver OOM, executor OOM, shuffle OOM and broadcast OOM
They are variants of the same JVM error
Executor heap OOM, container/pod kill, driver heap OOM, and Python worker memory — each has a different diagnosis path and different fixes
Heap OOM, metaspace OOM, direct buffer OOM and stack overflow
questions.explanation: Executor heap OOM throws and the task retries; a container kill leaves no exception and the process vanishes; a driver heap OOM kills the whole application with no recovery path; and a Python worker memory kill surfaces on the JVM side as an EOFException. Naming which one you have is most of the fix — and the wrong name sends you to a knob that makes things worse.

questions.prompt: Walk through your diagnostic path when a Spark job reports 'out of memory'.
questions.model_answer: First question: was an exception THROWN, or did a process VANISH? If thrown, read the stack to decide driver versus executor. A driver stack mentioning collect, toPandas, BroadcastExchange or plan objects means the coordinator was asked to hold too much — the fix is to stop collecting, cap the broadcast, or reduce task count, never simply more driver memory. An executor heap OOM sends me to the distribution question: is max task input far above the median? If yes it is skew and no amount of memory is sufficient; if it is uniform, raise parallelism or lower cores per executor, since per-task memory is roughly (heap x memory.fraction) / cores. If instead the process vanished — exit 137, OOMKilled, log ending mid-line — it is a container kill and the heap may be half empty, so the overflow is non-heap: in PySpark the prime suspect is Python worker processes, one per concurrent task; otherwise off-heap settings, native codecs or direct buffers. There the fixes are capping pyspark memory, reducing cores, or raising memoryOverhead AND the container together. Raising spark.executor.memory is roughly the tenth option, and it is actively wrong for a container kill because it grows the heap at the expense of the region that overflowed.
questions.explanation: The senior signal is the exception-versus-kill split first, the skew-versus-uniform split second, and knowing that more memory can trade an OOM for a GC-induced heartbeat timeout.

questions.prompt: An executor reports Task Time 4.2 h and GC Time 1.9 h. What is the reading, and what is the risk beyond slowness?
options: About 45% GC, which is normal for shuffle-heavy jobs
GC time overlaps task time, so the ratio is not meaningful
About 31% GC — acceptable if the job completes
About 45% GC — nearly half the paid time produced nothing, and a long pause can trigger a heartbeat timeout and executor loss
questions.explanation: GC% = JVM GC Time / Executor Run Time, computed per executor rather than cluster-wide. At ~45% the executor's useful throughput is roughly half what you pay for, and it is one long pause away from missing heartbeats — which is why GC problems often show up in the incident log as a FetchFailedException and get misdiagnosed as a network issue.

questions.prompt: Tasks in a stage get progressively slower as the stage runs, with no change in per-task input. What does this pattern suggest?
options: A growing live set — accumulating cached blocks or aggregation state — so collections take longer and recover less
Speculative execution competing for slots
The shuffle service throttling requests
Network congestion building up
questions.explanation: The signature of GC pressure is not that GC exists — it is that pauses GROW as the stage progresses. That growth means objects are accumulating: cached blocks, a large aggregation hash map, or objects being promoted faster than they die. A job that gets steadily slower without the data changing is the classic surface symptom.

questions.prompt: When is changing the JVM garbage collector an appropriate response?
options: As the first fix whenever GC time exceeds 10%
Only after workload-level causes are excluded and GC logs show pause behaviour, not live-set size, is the constraint
Whenever executors are lost to heartbeat timeouts
Whenever the heap exceeds 32 GB
questions.explanation: Collector settings change how efficiently the JVM manages a live set you have not yet tried to reduce. If an executor spends 45% of its time collecting because someone cached a 400 GB DataFrame that is read once, no collector setting fixes that. Exclude caching, object churn in UDFs, cores per executor and oversized heaps first; then, if you do change it, change one thing and write down why.

questions.prompt: Which of these most directly increases GC pressure on an executor?
options: Lowering spark.sql.files.maxPartitionBytes
Raising spark.sql.shuffle.partitions
Caching large datasets, which fills the old generation with long-lived objects the collector must scan and cannot free
Enabling adaptive query execution
questions.explanation: Cached blocks are long-lived by definition. Other major contributors: too many cores per executor (N concurrent tasks all allocating into one heap), row-at-a-time UDFs allocating per record, wide rows materialised as objects, oversized heaps (more to scan, longer worst-case pauses), and high-cardinality GROUP BY building enormous hash maps.

questions.prompt: Explain why giving a Spark executor MORE memory can make a job less stable.
questions.model_answer: Beyond a certain heap size the cost of collection rises: there is more to scan, and stop-the-world pauses get longer in the worst case. A pause long enough to miss heartbeats — the Apache default network timeout is 120s — causes the driver to declare the executor dead. Losing an executor destroys its shuffle output, because shuffle data is written to local disk and is not replicated, so Spark must re-run the map stage that produced it. That re-execution puts the same pressure back on the same cluster, and if the underlying cause is still present the cycle compounds into a retry storm. So the chain is: bigger heap -> longer pause -> heartbeat timeout -> executor loss -> FetchFailedException -> stage re-execution. You can genuinely trade a clean, retryable OOM for an expensive cascade. The better levers are usually reducing what each task must hold — more partitions, fewer cores per executor, less caching — rather than enlarging the heap.
questions.explanation: The senior signal is connecting heap size to pause duration to heartbeat loss to unreplicated shuffle output, rather than treating memory as monotonically good.

questions.prompt: A stage has 5,000 tasks; 4,998 finish in 45 seconds and two run for 40 minutes. What is the single most important thing to check next?
options: Whether speculative execution is enabled
The total shuffle write for the stage
The executor logs for those two tasks
Whether those two tasks also READ far more data than the median
questions.explanation: Input volume is the discriminator between the two candidate causes. If the slow tasks read ~100x more data, duration scales with work and it is skew — go find the hot key. If they read a normal amount and simply took longer, it is environmental: check whether they shared an executor or host, then GC time and host disk/network. Speculation helps the second case and is useless against the first.

questions.prompt: Which value is most often the single largest 'key' in a real fact table?
options: A sentinel such as -1, 0, 'UNKNOWN' or an empty string, emitted by upstream systems that refuse to write NULL
The primary key of the largest dimension
The most common customer ID
The most recent partition date
questions.explanation: Sentinels are the classic hidden hot key. NULL skew behaves similarly — every NULL hashes to the same partition — with an extra insult: in an INNER equi-join NULL keys never match, so those rows are shuffled across the network and then discarded. Profiling the key with counts and percentage-of-total surfaces both immediately.

questions.prompt: Adaptive skew-join handling is enabled, yet a 40-minute straggler persists. Which of these does NOT explain that?
options: The partition exceeds the relative factor but not the absolute byte threshold
Adaptive query execution only applies to DataFrame code, not Spark SQL
The skew is in a GROUP BY group rather than a join
The skew was created downstream by an explode()
questions.explanation: AQE applies to both the SQL and DataFrame paths — they share the same optimizer. The three real explanations: its skew handling targets skewed shuffle partitions in JOINS, so it does nothing for aggregation-group skew or for skew generated after the shuffle boundary by explode; and BOTH the relative factor and the absolute byte threshold must be exceeded, so a partition 40x the median can still be ignored. Skew on the READ side (one enormous input file) is a fourth case, before any shuffle exists to split.

questions.prompt: Why does `repartition(2000, hot_key)` fail to fix skew on that key?
options: Because AQE immediately coalesces the result
Because 2000 is too few partitions
Because hashing a hot value still sends every row carrying it to a single partition
Because repartition is a narrow transformation
questions.explanation: Hash partitioning is deterministic: all rows with the same key land together, by design — that is what makes joins and aggregations work. Repartitioning helps when the CURRENT partitioning is bad for an unrelated reason, or when you repartition on a different, better-distributed column. It also costs a full shuffle, so it must pay for itself.

questions.prompt: For which aggregation does salting NOT compose cleanly into a two-stage combine?
options: MAX
SUM
COUNT
An exact median
questions.explanation: Salting works for aggregations that are associative and can be combined from partial results: SUM, COUNT, MIN, MAX. An exact median (or an exact COUNT DISTINCT without a sketch) needs the full group together, so partial results per salt bucket cannot simply be merged. Approximate percentile functions and sketch-based distinct counts exist precisely to make these tractable at scale.

questions.prompt: When salting a JOIN (rather than an aggregation), what cost do you accept?
options: The other side must be replicated N ways, multiplying its size
The join can no longer use an equality condition
Output ordering becomes non-deterministic
The join result becomes approximate
questions.explanation: Salting the fact side spreads a hot key across N buckets, but every matching row on the dimension side must then exist in all N buckets — so the dimension is replicated N times. The spread factor is a real cost, not a free knob, and it is why isolating a small number of hot keys into a broadcast branch is often cheaper than salting the whole join.

questions.prompt: Why prefer a deterministic salt (for example a hash of a high-cardinality column) over `RAND()`?
options: It produces a more even spread in all cases
RAND() is non-deterministic, so a stage retry can repartition differently and make results harder to reproduce
RAND() is not supported inside a GROUP BY
Deterministic salts avoid the extra shuffle
questions.explanation: Determinism matters for reproducibility and for pipelines that must produce identical output across retries. The trade-off runs the other way on evenness: a deterministic salt is only as uniform as the column you hash, so pick something high-cardinality and uncorrelated with the join key — and then VERIFY the resulting distribution rather than assuming it.

questions.prompt: In an INNER equi-join, what happens to rows whose join key is NULL?
options: They are broadcast to every executor
They are matched against all rows on the other side
They are shuffled to a common partition and then discarded, because NULL never equals NULL
They are filtered out before the shuffle automatically
questions.explanation: This is pure waste: network transfer and one oversized partition, for rows that cannot survive the join. Filtering them before the exchange removes the largest partition entirely. The caveat is LEFT joins, where those rows must be retained — handle them in a separate branch and union the results back rather than dropping them.

questions.prompt: Which measure best predicts how expensive a hot key will be when records vary greatly in width?
options: Distinct count of the key
The number of partitions the key spans
Row count per key
Bytes per key
questions.explanation: Row counts are a proxy. When record width varies — a nested array column, a large JSON blob — a key with 200k wide rows can cost more than one with 2M narrow rows. Profiling bytes per key (or row count alongside average width) predicts partition size far better and avoids chasing the wrong key.

questions.prompt: Which are legitimate ways to address a skewed join? (Select all that apply.)
options: Filter out sentinel and NULL keys that cannot match
Split hot keys into a separate branch and broadcast the small side there
Salt the hot key and replicate the other side
Redesign the data model so the whale no longer shares the join key
Raise spark.task.maxFailures so skewed tasks get more attempts
questions.explanation: Filtering unmatched keys, isolating hot keys, salting, and redesigning the model all change the distribution or the work done per partition. Raising task retries does nothing for a task that is slow rather than failing — and if it IS failing, more attempts just pay for the same doomed work repeatedly. Each real remedy has limits worth stating: filtering only applies where those rows cannot contribute; the two-path pattern rescans unless you persist; salting costs replication; the model redesign is a quarter of work, not an afternoon.

questions.prompt: How do you PROVE a skew fix worked, rather than getting lucky?
options: The max/median ratio for duration AND shuffle read fell, and you noted the change in total shuffle bytes and executor-hours
No tasks failed on the retry
The stage now uses more executors
The job finished faster than the previous run
questions.explanation: Runtime can improve for unrelated reasons — a quieter cluster, a smaller input day. The distribution ratios are the mechanism. Also record total shuffle bytes and executor-hours, because some skew fixes (salting with replication, two-path scans) INCREASE total work while reducing wall clock. That may be the right trade, but you must know you made it.

questions.prompt: Which of these produces skew that adaptive skew-join handling cannot address at all?
options: A hot merchant_id in a fact-to-dimension join
One input Parquet file that is far larger than the rest, before any shuffle exists
A NULL-heavy join key
A moderately uneven distribution across shuffle partitions
questions.explanation: AQE reasons about SHUFFLE partitions — it observes their real sizes after a stage completes and can split ones that qualify. A skewed input file is a read-side problem that occurs before any shuffle boundary, so there is nothing for it to split. Fixes there are file-layout ones: compaction, splitting the file, or adjusting maxPartitionBytes if the file is splittable.

questions.prompt: A job is stuck at 99% with two long-running tasks. Walk through your investigation and remediation.
questions.model_answer: First I separate skew from straggler, because they share a symptom and share almost no fixes. I open the task table, find the two tasks, and compare their input and shuffle-read bytes to the median. If they read ~100x more, duration scales with work and it is skew. If they read a normal amount, it is environmental — I check whether both ran on the same executor or host, then that executor's GC ratio and the host's disk and network metrics; a degraded disk produces exactly this. For skew, I profile the key with a GROUP BY key, COUNT(*), and percentage-of-total, looking specifically for sentinels like -1, 0 or 'UNKNOWN' and for NULL, and I check bytes per key as well as row count if records vary in width. Then I choose by what the profile shows: if the hot value cannot match (a sentinel or NULL in an inner join) I filter it before the exchange, which deletes the biggest partition outright; if a handful of genuine whale keys dominate, I isolate them into a separate branch where the small side can be broadcast, and union back; if the aggregation is additive I salt with a two-stage combine, using a deterministic salt for reproducibility. I also check whether AQE skew handling engaged at all, since it needs both its relative factor and its absolute byte threshold exceeded, and it does nothing for aggregation-group skew or explode-generated skew. I verify by the max/median ratio for duration AND shuffle read falling, not by runtime alone, and I record total shuffle bytes and executor-hours because salting trades total work for wall clock. Prevention is a daily key-distribution check alerting when any single value exceeds a set share of rows.
questions.explanation: The senior signal is the input-size discriminator first, naming sentinel and NULL keys specifically, and verifying against the distribution ratio rather than runtime.

questions.prompt: What is the Apache Spark default for `spark.sql.shuffle.partitions`?
options: It is derived from input size
The total number of executor cores
questions.explanation: 200 is the Apache default. Note that `spark.default.parallelism` — which defaults to the total number of cores in cluster mode — governs RDD operations, NOT DataFrame/SQL shuffles. Setting the latter and expecting SQL shuffles to change is a common source of confusion.

questions.prompt: Which four physical resources does a single shuffle consume simultaneously?
options: CPU, memory, network and driver heap
Memory, disk, network and the metastore
CPU, disk, network and the external shuffle service
CPU, memory, disk and network
questions.explanation: Map side: partition by key, sort within partition, serialize and compress (CPU), buffer (memory), write data and index files to LOCAL disk. Reduce side: fetch each partition's block from every map executor (network), buffer in execution memory, spill if it does not fit. A fifth cost is durability: map output must survive until consumed, or the map stage re-runs.

questions.prompt: With AQE enabled, how should you think about `spark.sql.shuffle.partitions`?
options: It is the INITIAL count before coalescing — set it generously, because coalescing only merges and skew splitting applies only to qualifying partitions
It should be set as low as possible to reduce scheduling overhead
It should exactly match the number of executor cores
It is ignored entirely
questions.explanation: AQE moves the tuning unit from a COUNT to a SIZE. Coalescing merges small post-shuffle partitions toward the advisory size; skew handling can split a partition that clears both its relative and absolute conditions. Neither rescues a stage where every partition is uniformly oversized — so too low is worse than too high, and the real dial is the advisory partition size.

questions.prompt: What is the Apache default for `spark.sql.adaptive.advisoryPartitionSizeInBytes`?
options: 8 MB
64 MB
128 MB
256 MB
questions.explanation: 64 MB. This is the most useful AQE knob because it expresses the target as a SIZE rather than a count — raise it for wide, cheap rows; lower it for expensive per-row work. Watch that a large advisory size can silently undo an increase in the initial partition count by coalescing straight back.

questions.prompt: From which Spark version is `spark.sql.adaptive.enabled` true by default?
questions.explanation: AQE was introduced in 3.0 but was OFF by default there and in 3.1; it became enabled by default in 3.2.0. On 3.0/3.1 the older fixed-partition-count tuning advice still applies. Always confirm it is actually on in your run — legacy job configs frequently disable it.

questions.prompt: A stage shows 200 tasks, median shuffle read 7.8 GB, max ~8.1 GB, and 9 TB of disk spill. What is the diagnosis?
options: A slow local disk on one host
An expensive Python UDF in the stage
Severe data skew on the join key
Uniform under-partitioning — every partition exceeds the execution memory each task gets
questions.explanation: Max ~= median rules out skew. Enormous per-task input plus multi-TB spill says every partition is too big for its share of execution memory — roughly (heap x memory.fraction) / cores. The fix is more partitions (and an advisory size low enough that AQE does not coalesce them back), or fewer cores per executor. The confirming metric is spill going to ZERO, not runtime falling.

questions.prompt: A stage has 240,000 tasks with a median duration of 40 ms and the driver's CPU is pinned. What is happening?
options: Over-partitioning — per-task scheduling overhead exceeds useful work, and the driver is the bottleneck
The shuffle service is throttling fetches
GC pressure on the driver from cached blocks
The executors are under-provisioned
questions.explanation: Tasks shorter than their own scheduling overhead mean you are paying coordination cost for nothing, and the driver must track metadata for every one of them. Ensure AQE coalescing is enabled and raise the advisory partition size. Watch median task duration as the signal: once it is in the tens of milliseconds, you have gone too far in that direction.

questions.prompt: Why does an `Exchange` node in a physical plan not automatically indicate a problem?
options: Exchanges are always removed by AQE at runtime
Any large join, wide aggregation or window over a key requires equal keys to be co-located — that is what an Exchange does
Exchange nodes are logical only and cost nothing
Exchanges only move metadata, not data
questions.explanation: Removing exchanges is not a goal in itself — a job with zero exchanges that scans ten times more data is slower. An Exchange deserves attention when it is AVOIDABLE (a broadcast would do, or the data is already partitioned compatibly), OVERSIZED (you are shuffling columns nothing downstream reads), or REPEATED (computed twice because reuse failed). Those three questions, not the word itself, are the diagnosis.

questions.prompt: Total shuffle write is 2.1 TB for a job whose input is 2 TB, joining a large fact to an 80 MB dimension. What should you check first?
options: Whether compression is enabled on shuffle output
Whether the shuffle partition count is too low
Whether the join is a SortMergeJoin that should have been a broadcast — typically because statistics are missing or stale
Whether local disks are fast enough for that volume
questions.explanation: Shuffling the fact table to join an 80 MB dimension is work that should not exist. If the SQL tab shows the build side is genuinely tiny but the plan chose sort-merge, the size ESTIMATE was wrong — usually missing statistics. Running ANALYZE TABLE ... COMPUTE STATISTICS and confirming the plan converts is a far bigger win than any partition-count tuning. The best shuffle optimization is the shuffle you delete.

questions.prompt: What does `spark.default.parallelism` control?
options: The maximum number of concurrent tasks per executor
The initial executor count under dynamic allocation
The number of partitions produced by DataFrame and SQL shuffles
The default partition count for RDD operations — it does NOT govern SQL/DataFrame shuffles
questions.explanation: This trips people up in a specific way: someone sets spark.default.parallelism, sees no change in a DataFrame job, and concludes the setting 'does not work'. Modern pipeline code is almost all DataFrame or SQL, where spark.sql.shuffle.partitions applies. If RDD operations are mixed in, or a library drops to RDDs, both are live at once.

questions.prompt: What does the `AQEShuffleRead` node in the SQL tab tell you?
options: What AQE actually decided at runtime — coalescing and skew-split counts
That the shuffle output was cached
That the stage was retried
That the shuffle was read from an external shuffle service
questions.explanation: Its presence confirms AQE acted, and its metrics show what it did. This is the only way to see AQE's decisions — a static EXPLAIN cannot show them, because they are made using statistics that only exist after a stage completes.

questions.prompt: Why is a fetch failure disproportionately expensive compared with other task failures?
options: It always aborts the job immediately
Shuffle output is not replicated, so losing the producing executor forces re-execution of the map stage that created it
It forces a full re-read of the source data
It invalidates all cached blocks cluster-wide
questions.explanation: Map output lives on the producing executor's local disk. When that executor is gone, the data is gone, and Spark must re-run the map tasks that produced it — potentially an hour of upstream work on a large job. That re-execution then puts the same pressure back on the same cluster. This is also why an external shuffle service changes the economics: it decouples shuffle data from executor lifetime.

questions.prompt: Which metric should determine the right shuffle partition SIZE for a given stage?
options: The ratio of shuffle write to shuffle read
The number of executors
Spill — zero spill with tasks comfortably longer than a few seconds means the size is right
The input file count
questions.explanation: A partition's cost depends on how much memory its rows occupy while being processed, how expensive each row is, how well it compresses, and how much execution memory each task actually gets — none of which are constants across workloads. Spill says partitions are too big for the memory available; median durations in the tens of milliseconds say they are too small. Any single universal number is implicitly assuming one workload shape.

questions.prompt: Which are genuine costs of setting the shuffle partition count very high? (Select all that apply.)
options: Per-task scheduling overhead becomes a significant fraction of useful work
The number of shuffle blocks grows as maps x reducers, producing many tiny reads
The driver tracks more task metadata
Writes can produce many small output files
Each partition is more likely to spill to disk
questions.explanation: Scheduling overhead, the maps-times-reducers block explosion, extra driver metadata and tiny output files are all real costs of over-partitioning. Spill is the opposite failure — it comes from partitions that are too LARGE for the memory each task gets, so a higher partition count reduces spill rather than causing it. That asymmetry is why a generous initial count plus AQE coalescing is the safer default.

questions.prompt: What does `spark.sql.adaptive.coalescePartitions.enabled` (Apache default true) make safe?
options: Broadcasting larger tables
Running with fewer executors than partitions
Disabling the external shuffle service
Setting a generous INITIAL shuffle partition count, since small partitions get merged toward the advisory size
questions.explanation: Coalescing is what turns 'set it high and let AQE reduce it' from reckless into standard practice. Without it, a generous initial count leaves you with the full number of small partitions and all the scheduling overhead that implies.

questions.prompt: A stage spills 9 TB to disk. Walk from that number to a validated fix.
questions.model_answer: First I establish whether the spill is uniform or concentrated, because that changes everything. I compare max task input against median: if they are close, every partition is too big and it is a sizing problem; if the spill is concentrated in a few tasks, it is skew and partition count will not help. Assuming uniform, I do the arithmetic — per-task execution memory is roughly (usable heap x spark.memory.fraction) / spark.executor.cores — and compare that against the median partition size. If a 16 GB heap with 5 cores gives each task on the order of a couple of GB and the median partition is 7.8 GB, spill is inevitable rather than incidental. The fix is one variable: raise the initial shuffle partition count so partitions start small enough, and lower the advisory partition size so AQE does not coalesce them straight back into the same problem — those are two settings but one mechanism, the partition-size target. Halving cores per executor is the alternative lever, since it doubles per-task memory at no extra cost. I predict before running: median task input should fall roughly proportionally, spill should approach zero, and stage duration should fall by more than half. Then I measure the SAME metrics I captured as a baseline. The confirming metric is spill going to zero — not runtime, which can improve for unrelated reasons. I also watch two side effects: task count rises, and output file count rises with it, so I may add a REBALANCE before the write to keep file sizes sane. Finally I add 'any disk spill on this stage' to the health scorecard so the failure becomes a monitored condition rather than oral tradition.
questions.explanation: The senior signal is the uniform-versus-concentrated split, the per-task memory arithmetic, and validating on spill rather than runtime.

questions.prompt: What is the Apache default for `spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold`?
options: 10 MB
100 MB
It is disabled by default
1 MB
questions.explanation: 10 MB. Two subtleties matter more than the number: it is compared against an ESTIMATE, not a measurement; and the estimate concerns the size in Spark's internal representation, not the compressed file size on disk — a 10 MB Parquet file can expand well beyond 10 MB in memory.

questions.prompt: In a BroadcastHashJoin, where does the build side physically go?
options: Directly from storage to each executor
Collected to the DRIVER first, then shipped to every executor
Into the external shuffle service
Into a replicated cache on the cluster manager
questions.explanation: This is why a broadcast join is effectively a collect() you did not write, and why raising the broadcast threshold globally increases driver memory pressure for every join in every query. It is also why spark.sql.broadcastTimeout (Apache default 300s) exists and why timeout warnings are an early signal that the build side is growing.

questions.prompt: A pipeline that ran for 18 months starts failing with a driver OOM during a broadcast exchange. The code has not changed. What is the most likely cause?
options: The dimension table's statistics became stale
The driver's memory allocation was reduced
An explicit BROADCAST hint overrides the size check, and the hinted table has grown well past what fits
AQE started converting the join to a broadcast
questions.explanation: A hint tells Spark 'trust me, this is small', and nothing re-checks it next quarter. A table hinted at 6 MB that has grown to 40 million rows will take the driver down. Every broadcast hint in a long-lived pipeline should be paired with a size assertion or a row-count alert. Broadcast-timeout warnings in earlier runs are the early warning that usually gets ignored.

questions.prompt: Why is SortMergeJoin described as robust for large equi-joins?
options: It never requires sorting when inputs are bucketed
It automatically handles skewed keys
It avoids shuffling either side
The sort lets it spill to disk and keep going, so it degrades rather than failing
questions.explanation: SortMergeJoin shuffles both sides by key, sorts each partition, and merges. The sort is what makes it degrade gracefully under memory pressure. ShuffledHashJoin avoids the sort by building a hash map from one side's partition — faster when it fits, but far less graceful under skew, because one oversized partition simply will not fit.

questions.prompt: Seeing `BroadcastNestedLoopJoin` in a plan should prompt what reaction?
options: Investigate: it means no usable equality condition, so comparison count scales with the product of the inputs
Increase the broadcast threshold so it becomes a hash join
Enable AQE so it can be converted at runtime
None — it is an optimisation for small tables
questions.explanation: It appears when the join condition is non-equi (BETWEEN, <, LIKE) or missing entirely. Even when the OUTPUT is small, the work is O(left x right) comparisons — 1M x 50k is 50 billion. The usual fix is to add an equality component (a bucket, a date key) so a hash join becomes possible, then apply the range predicate as a filter.

questions.prompt: `orders` has 100M rows and joins `dim_customer` on customer_id. Output is 500M rows. What happened?
options: The join produced a cartesian product
The dimension has ~5 rows per customer_id — an SCD2 history not filtered to current, or a duplicate load
The fact table was read five times
AQE split skewed partitions, duplicating rows
questions.explanation: A clean 5x is multiplication, not growth — organic growth is not a round multiple. Test with GROUP BY key HAVING COUNT(*) > 1 on the dimension. Critically, this is a CORRECTNESS incident as much as a performance one: every downstream aggregate has been 5x too high since it started, so the response includes finding what published on top of it.

questions.prompt: Which single ratio best detects join fan-out automatically?
options: GC time divided by task time
Shuffle write divided by input bytes
Output rows divided by input rows, tracked against its own baseline
Task count divided by executor count
questions.explanation: Output-per-input-row catches the whole class — duplicate dimension keys, an SCD2 filter that was dropped, an unbounded explode. It belongs on the pipeline health scorecard alongside input bytes, because the performance symptom and the correctness bug are the SAME event.

questions.prompt: Statistics on a dimension were reset by a maintenance operation. What is the likely consequence?
options: Partition pruning stops working
AQE is disabled for that table
Queries fail with an AnalysisException
Size estimates fall back to a much larger raw footprint, so a broadcast join can become a sort-merge join and shuffle volume explodes
questions.explanation: The optimizer picks broadcast from an estimate. With no statistics, the estimate can be wildly wrong in either direction. A 6-minute query becoming 71 minutes with shuffle write rising from 40 GB to 2.1 TB — on unchanged data — is the classic signature. Fix is ANALYZE TABLE ... COMPUTE STATISTICS, then confirm the plan reverts on its own rather than pinning it with a hint.

questions.prompt: Why collect COLUMN statistics in addition to table statistics?
options: They provide distinct counts, min/max and null counts, which let the optimizer estimate SELECTIVITY rather than just size
They enable adaptive query execution
They are needed for broadcast joins to work at all
Column statistics are required for partition pruning
questions.explanation: Table statistics give row count and total size, enabling size-based strategy choice. Column statistics let the optimizer estimate how much a predicate reduces a relation, which drives join ordering and intermediate-size estimates. Note that cost-based optimization and CBO join reordering are both DISABLED by default in Apache Spark and depend on these statistics — turning CBO on without them changes nothing useful.

questions.prompt: Why can a query broadcast correctly in development on a 1% sample but choose sort-merge in production?
options: Sampling changes the join type explicitly
The build side crosses the broadcast threshold at full scale, so production runs a fundamentally different physical plan that dev never tested
Production disables AQE by default
Sample data is always cached
questions.explanation: This is a THRESHOLD being crossed, which is why the failure is discontinuous rather than gradual. It is also why 'works on a sample, dies at full scale' should trigger a PLAN comparison rather than a volume comparison: skew is invisible at 1%, per-partition memory scales, and cardinality effects multiply. Compare the two plans first — a plan difference explains most of these instantly.

questions.prompt: Which are legitimate reasons a join produces far more rows than expected? (Select all that apply.)
options: Duplicate keys in the dimension table
An SCD2 dimension not filtered to the current record
A missing predicate producing a cartesian product
Many-to-many relationships on both sides
The shuffle partition count being too low
questions.explanation: Duplicate dimension keys, an unfiltered SCD2 history, a missing predicate and many-to-many relationships are all cardinality mechanisms. Partition count affects how work is DIVIDED, never how many rows the join produces — a common confusion that sends people to a tuning knob when they have a correctness bug. Output rows are a function of the data and the join condition, not the parallelism.

questions.prompt: When is `spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold = -1` a defensible setting?
options: Whenever AQE is enabled
Whenever broadcasts cause any driver pressure
As a diagnostic to confirm broadcasts are the cause of driver instability, or where estimates are systematically unreliable
On any cluster with fewer than 50 executors
questions.explanation: Setting it to -1 disables auto-broadcast entirely — useful as an experiment, and occasionally as a blunt production setting where no statistics exist and estimates keep choosing broadcast for things that are not small. The cost is that EVERY join now shuffles, including the ones where broadcast was correct and valuable, so it usually trades one incident for a permanent tax. Targeted alternatives: fix statistics, lower rather than disable the threshold, or hint the specific offending join.

questions.prompt: How do you determine which join strategy a query actually used, and what would you do if it is not the one you expected?
questions.model_answer: I look at the SQL tab of the FINISHED run rather than a static EXPLAIN, because with AQE enabled the plan is re-optimised at runtime — a sort-merge join can be promoted to a broadcast once real shuffle sizes are measured, so the pre-execution plan is a proposal and only the executed plan is authoritative. In the join node I read the strategy and the build-side size metric. If it is sort-merge and I expected broadcast, I compare that measured size against spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold and ask why the ESTIMATE was wrong. Two common gaps: statistics are missing or stale, so the estimate came from a raw footprint far larger than reality; or the build side sits behind a filter whose selectivity the optimizer cannot estimate without column statistics. My first move is ANALYZE TABLE ... COMPUTE STATISTICS, including FOR COLUMNS on the join and filter keys, then re-run and confirm the plan converts on its own — that fixes the decision everywhere rather than at one call site. I reach for a BROADCAST hint only as a last resort, because a hint overrides the safety check, and I pair it with a size assertion or a row-count alert on that table, since a hinted table that quietly grows is how you turn a slow job into a driver OOM. I would also check the reverse case: a plan that broadcasts something it should not, where the honest fix is removing the hint rather than raising driver memory.
questions.explanation: The senior signal is treating the SQL tab as authoritative over EXPLAIN, fixing statistics before hints, and knowing a hint is a promise someone has to keep.

questions.prompt: Why is a driver failure more serious than an executor failure?
options: Driver failures corrupt the output data
Executor failures are always retried automatically, driver failures never are
Drivers are more expensive to provision
Spark recovers from executor loss by re-running work; losing the driver kills the application with no recovery path
questions.explanation: The asymmetry is structural. Executor loss costs re-execution — expensive, but recoverable. The driver holds the DAG, all task metadata, every broadcast build side and anything collected; it is one JVM, one heap, and there is no failover. That is why almost every catastrophic Spark failure is a driver failure even though almost every tuning conversation is about executors.

questions.prompt: A job runs 50 minutes, all stages green, then fails and the output table is empty. Where do you look?
options: The driver — the failure is after all distributed work, which localises it immediately
The last executor to be removed
The shuffle service logs
Storage permissions on the output path
questions.explanation: All stages complete with no failed tasks means the distributed work succeeded. Anything failing after that is the driver: a collect(), a toPandas(), the result-size guard, or the write commit. The classic culprit is a validation helper such as `len(df.collect()) > 0` that was harmless when the output was 40,000 rows and is fatal now that it is 90 million.

questions.prompt: Why is `toPandas()` more dangerous on the driver than `collect()`?
options: It bypasses spark.driver.maxResultSize
The data lands in the driver's JVM and is then converted into the driver's Python process, so you need room for both representations
It always disables Arrow optimisation
It runs on a single executor before transferring
questions.explanation: You pay twice, concurrently. Arrow-based conversion makes the transfer far more efficient, but efficiency is not capacity — an efficient transfer of 40 GB into an 8 GB driver still fails. If the answer is 'but I need all the rows in pandas', the pipeline design is the problem, not the memory setting.

questions.prompt: A stage has millions of tasks. Beyond scheduling overhead, what specific driver risk does that create?
options: Broadcast variables must be re-sent per task
Increased shuffle block count on executors
The driver holds metadata and accumulator updates for every task, so it becomes both a heap and a CPU bottleneck
The event log grows too large to write
questions.explanation: At tens of thousands of tasks this is invisible; at millions it is a heap problem and a scheduler-thread problem simultaneously. The tell is low executor CPU with high driver CPU and executors idle waiting for work. The fix is partition sizing or file layout — raising driver memory only postpones it.

questions.prompt: A backfill provisions 500 executors, runs 9 hours at ~6% cluster CPU, and the Jobs tab shows 4,380 separate jobs. What is the cause?
options: Dynamic allocation is thrashing executors
Object-store throttling on the output prefix
The shuffle partition count is far too low
A loop in driver code submitting one action per iteration — each is a full job with plan compilation, scheduling and teardown
questions.explanation: Thousands of tiny jobs means the driver is the constraint and the executors were never the bottleneck. The fix is to express the loop as DATA — read the whole date range in one job with the date as a column, write partitioned output in a single action. Requesting more executors makes it worse by giving the same driver more to track.

questions.prompt: There is a multi-minute gap between job submission and the first task starting, with no active stage. What is the most likely cause?
options: The driver is listing files or compiling a very large plan before any task can run
The first stage is waiting on a broadcast
The event log is being initialised
Executors are still being provisioned
questions.explanation: On object storage, listing a table with a very large number of files or partition directories means a very large number of API calls, and it happens on the driver before a single task runs. Deep plans with many unions or wide CTEs can also make plan compilation take minutes. Both look identical from the outside: an application that is 'running' while nothing happens.

questions.prompt: Which symptoms together indicate a driver bottleneck rather than an executor one? (Select all that apply.)
options: Active tasks far below total slots while the job is 'running'
Driver CPU pinned at 100%
Long gaps between stages with no stage active
Hundreds or thousands of tiny jobs in the Jobs tab
High disk spill in the dominant stage
questions.explanation: Idle slots, pinned driver CPU, timeline gaps with no active stage, and a flood of tiny jobs all say work is not reaching the executors or the coordinator is saturated. Disk spill is an executor-side memory symptom — it means partitions exceed per-task execution memory, which is a distribution and sizing problem. Mixing the two is how people end up adding executors to a driver-bound job and making it slower.

questions.prompt: Contrast an executor problem with a driver problem, and explain why the distinction changes what you do.
questions.model_answer: An executor problem is 'the distributed work is too heavy': its symptoms scale with DATA — partition size, skew, join strategy, file layout, memory per task — and adding executors can genuinely help, because there is more parallelisable work than there are slots. A driver problem is 'the coordinator is being asked to do too much': its symptoms scale with TASK COUNT, FILE COUNT and RESULT SIZE — millions of tasks whose metadata fills the driver heap, millions of files that must be listed before any stage starts, a collect() or toPandas() returning a distributed dataset to one machine, a broadcast build side that grew, an enormous query plan, or a loop submitting thousands of small jobs. The distinction changes everything because the fixes are opposite in direction: for the driver case, adding executors makes it strictly WORSE, since more executors means more tasks for the same single-threaded coordinator to schedule and track. The diagnostic is cheap: if executors are alive but mostly idle while the job is 'running', if there are long gaps in the timeline with no active stage, and if driver CPU is pinned, stop thinking about executor capacity and go look at task count, file count, and what the code returns to the driver. Note too that the driver has no failover — losing it kills the application mid-write — so driver-side limits like spark.driver.maxResultSize are guards worth keeping rather than raising.
questions.explanation: The senior signal is naming the scaling variable for each (data versus task/file/result count) and stating that scale-out actively harms the driver case.

questions.prompt: Which plan node marks a row-at-a-time Python UDF boundary?
options: ArrowEvalPython
BatchEvalPython
Generate
ObjectHashAggregate
questions.explanation: BatchEvalPython indicates row-at-a-time evaluation; ArrowEvalPython indicates the vectorised, Arrow-based path where data crosses in batches. Seeing either tells you rows are leaving the JVM; seeing BatchEvalPython tells you that you are also paying per-row serialization.

questions.prompt: Replacing a SQL CASE expression with a Python UDF took a job from 12 minutes to 3 hours. Beyond serialization cost, what else likely happened?
options: The UDF caused every partition to be cached
The UDF forced a shuffle
