The UDF is an optimizer barrier, so a predicate that used to be pushed into the scan no longer is — turning a pruned read into a much larger one
Python UDFs disable whole-stage code generation cluster-wide
questions.explanation: There are two separate costs and the second is usually the larger. Mechanically, each row moves to a Python worker and back, and the fused loop is cut into pieces around the UDF node. At the optimizer level the UDF is a black box: Catalyst cannot push a filter through it, eliminate it for rows that do not matter, or reorder around it. Check whether PushedFilters changed — that regression can dwarf the serialization cost.

questions.prompt: Why do pandas/Arrow UDFs generally outperform row-at-a-time Python UDFs?
options: They are visible to the Catalyst optimizer
They avoid launching Python worker processes
They execute inside the JVM
Data crosses to Python in Arrow batches, so serialization is paid per batch rather than per row
questions.explanation: The transfer cost drops dramatically. But two things do NOT change: the UDF is still opaque to the optimizer, so filters still cannot be pushed through it; and batch size now drives memory — a large batch times many concurrent workers is a container-kill risk, since Python worker memory lives outside the JVM heap.

questions.prompt: How do you establish that a stage is CPU-bound rather than memory- or I/O-bound?
options: Uniform task durations, zero spill, near-zero shuffle read blocked time, modest input bytes, and CPU time close to task duration
Task count far exceeding executor slots
Shuffle write greatly exceeding shuffle read
High GC time with low spill
questions.explanation: You infer CPU-bound from what is ABSENT. Uniform durations rule out skew; zero spill rules out memory pressure; near-zero blocked time rules out the network; modest input with long duration rules out I/O volume. CPU time ~= duration is the confirmation. Then look in the plan for the per-row operator: a UDF, a regex, a JSON function, or a window.

questions.prompt: A query calls `get_json_object` three times on the same column to extract three fields. What is the better pattern?
options: Cache the DataFrame before the extractions
Parse once into a typed struct with an explicit schema, then select fields
Increase the shuffle partition count so parsing parallelises
Move the extraction into a Python UDF
questions.explanation: Per-row JSON parsing is expensive, and three calls can mean three parses. Common-subexpression elimination helps but is not guaranteed for every expression shape. Parsing once into a struct also lets the engine prune fields it does not need. Verify by watching stage CPU time fall with input and output unchanged.

questions.prompt: What is the risk of three different window specifications in one SELECT?
options: Window functions force a broadcast join
Window functions cannot be combined in one query
Each distinct specification implies its own exchange and sort, so you pay the shuffle three times instead of once
The optimizer will silently drop two of them
questions.explanation: Sharing one specification across several expressions collapses them into a single pass. Also watch the partition key itself: PARTITION BY a low-cardinality column such as country, in a business concentrated in one country, is skew by construction.

questions.prompt: Which contribute meaningfully to CPU cost in a Spark stage? (Select all that apply.)
options: Backtracking regular expressions over billions of rows
Per-row JSON parsing
A heavy compression codec on a CPU-bound stage
Unbounded window frames
Increasing spark.sql.shuffle.partitions
questions.explanation: Backtracking regexes, per-row JSON parsing, a heavy codec on a CPU-bound stage and unbounded window frames are all per-row or per-partition computational costs. Partition count changes how work is DIVIDED, not how much per-row computation exists — the total CPU is roughly the same, spread over more tasks. On codecs specifically: heavier compression trades CPU for I/O, which is exactly backwards on a stage that is already CPU-bound.

questions.prompt: When is a Python UDF the right choice despite its costs?
questions.model_answer: When the logic genuinely has no native equivalent — a specialised algorithm, a domain library, a model call — and rewriting it in SQL would be either impossible or so convoluted that correctness suffers. The cost hierarchy is a tendency, not a law: a well-written Python UDF over a small, already-filtered set can easily beat a monstrous native expression tree, and an ill-conceived native regex over a billion rows is worse than either. The discipline is to make the choice deliberately and then reduce its blast radius: filter BEFORE the UDF so it sees as few rows as possible, since the optimizer cannot push predicates through it and will not do this for you; prefer an Arrow/pandas UDF so serialization is paid per batch rather than per row, while remembering that batch size now drives Python worker memory and that workers live outside the JVM heap; and watch cores per executor, because there is one worker process per concurrent task. I would also verify from the plan that PushedFilters on the source scan did not change when the UDF was introduced — that regression is often larger than the UDF's own cost and is easy to miss.
questions.explanation: The senior signal is refusing the absolute rule, then naming the specific mitigations: filter first, batch the boundary, watch worker count and check pushdown did not regress.

questions.prompt: What is the Apache default for `spark.sql.files.maxPartitionBytes`?
options: 256 MB
1 GB
32 MB
128 MB
questions.explanation: 128 MB. It is the target bytes per read partition when splitting files, which is why large SPLITTABLE files do not reduce parallelism — Spark divides them. The exception worth checking is a large file in a non-splittable compression format, which becomes exactly one task.

questions.prompt: Reading 150 GB stored as 50,000 files takes 25 minutes; the same data in ~300 files takes 4. Which cost is usually LARGEST?
options: Listing plus per-file open and footer reads — metadata cost scales with FILE COUNT, not data size
Network transfer of the additional bytes
Shuffle write amplification
CPU spent decompressing more blocks
questions.explanation: Four costs stack up: driver-side listing of 50,000 objects before any task starts; a footer read per file; poorer compression and encoding because 3 MB row groups are too small for dictionary and run-length encoding to work well; and scheduling overhead from thousands of tasks doing milliseconds of work each. A fifth, subtler one: per-file statistics over 3 MB are too coarse to skip anything, so predicate pushdown stops helping.

questions.prompt: What does `spark.sql.files.openCostInBytes` (Apache default 4 MB) actually do?
options: Rejects files smaller than 4 MB
Models the cost of opening a file, in bytes, so Spark packs small files into read partitions accordingly
Sets the minimum Parquet row-group size on write
Controls the read-ahead buffer size
questions.explanation: It is a MODELLING parameter, not a limit. Raising it makes Spark pack MORE small files into each task, which helps on high-latency object storage. It is a legitimate interim mitigation for a small-file problem — but it does nothing about listing cost, so it treats a symptom while the real fix is compaction plus fixing the writer.

questions.prompt: Which three distinct optimizations does columnar storage enable, and what does each skip?
options: Broadcast, shuffle and sort avoidance
Compression, encryption and caching
Partition pruning (skips directories), predicate pushdown / data skipping (skips row groups), and column pruning (skips columns)
Vectorisation, bucketing and sorting
questions.explanation: They are frequently conflated but fail independently. Verify each separately in the scan node: PartitionFilters populated for directory pruning, PushedFilters populated for row-group skipping, and ReadSchema listing only the columns you need for projection. An empty PartitionFilters on a partitioned table is the expensive one.

questions.prompt: Why is `SELECT *` particularly costly on a wide columnar table?
options: It disables predicate pushdown entirely
It prevents the vectorised reader from being used
It forces a full table lock
It defeats projection pushdown, so you read every column off storage and carry them through every exchange
questions.explanation: Columnar formats let you read only the columns you name. SELECT * reads all of them, then shuffles bytes nothing downstream looks at — frequently a 5-20x difference in bytes scanned and shuffled on a wide table. It also makes the query fragile: a new upstream column silently changes your output schema.

questions.prompt: Which characteristics of cloud object storage most change Spark debugging instincts?
options: Listing is an API call scaling with object count, every open has real latency, and throughput can be per-prefix
Reads are always slower than HDFS regardless of layout
Object stores do not support columnar formats efficiently
Files are immutable, so caching is unnecessary
questions.explanation: Listing cost is the invisible minutes before a job starts. Per-open latency is nothing for one file and everything for 50,000. And per-prefix throughput means a layout concentrating reads on one prefix can throttle even at modest total volume. Data locality, meanwhile, is largely moot — there is no local replica to schedule near, so ANY locality is normal rather than a finding.

questions.prompt: A table partitioned by `(ds, customer_id)` with 4 million customers spends 14 minutes before the first task runs. What is wrong?
options: The partition columns are in the wrong order
customer_id is a high-cardinality partition key, creating an unbounded number of directories that must be listed on every query
Statistics are missing on the table
The files are too large to split
questions.explanation: This is the most common irreversible modelling mistake: partitioning by a high-cardinality column creates millions of directories, most holding one tiny file, so listing dominates every query regardless of how selective the filter is. The fix is partitioning by ds only and serving the customer access pattern with clustering/sorting and statistics inside each day.

questions.prompt: Why can a partitioned table also be UNDER-partitioned?
options: Because statistics cannot be collected
Because too few partitions cause skew
Because with no useful partition column, every query must scan the whole table regardless of how selective its filter is
Because AQE cannot coalesce read partitions
questions.explanation: Partitioning is a band, not a direction. Too many partitions means listing cost and tiny files; too few — or partitioning on a column nobody filters on — means no pruning is possible and every query is a full scan. Partition on what queries actually filter on, and keep the cardinality bounded.

questions.prompt: Which are effective ways to prevent a small-file problem at the source? (Select all that apply.)
options: Control the output partition count before the write
Use a REBALANCE hint so AQE targets an even output size
Run compaction as a scheduled maintenance job
Use coalesce(10) immediately before writing
Reduce the number of storage partitions written into per run
questions.explanation: Output file count is (partitions at write time) x (storage partitions written into) — 4,000 shuffle partitions into 200 date partitions can mean 800,000 files. REBALANCE lets AQE size partitions rather than you guessing. coalesce is the trap: because it avoids a shuffle it cannot create a stage boundary, so reduced parallelism propagates BACKWARD through the whole preceding stage.

questions.prompt: Explain why 150 GB in 50,000 files and 150 GB in 300 files are not the same job.
questions.model_answer: The bytes are identical; the OVERHEAD is 50,000 times a fixed cost. First, listing: the driver must enumerate every object before any task starts, and on object storage that is API-call latency you cannot parallelise away because it happens on the coordinator — you see it as a long gap before the first stage. Second, per-file open and footer read: Parquet metadata cost scales with file count rather than data size, so you pay 50,000 footer reads for the same data. Third, compression and encoding efficiency: 3 MB files have tiny row groups, so dictionary and run-length encoding barely work and you physically transfer more bytes for the same information. Fourth, scheduling: with file-count-driven partitioning you get thousands of tasks each doing milliseconds of work, so per-task overhead becomes a real fraction and the driver tracks all of it. Fifth and subtlest, statistics granularity: min/max over a 3 MB file are too coarse to skip anything, so predicate pushdown quietly stops helping. The fix is compaction plus fixing whatever writer produces that layout — commonly a micro-batch committing every couple of minutes. Raising spark.sql.files.openCostInBytes makes Spark pack more small files per task and is a reasonable interim mitigation, but it does nothing about listing, so it is not the cure. Conversely files can be too big: a very large file in a non-splittable codec becomes exactly one task, so the target is a size band, not a maximum.
questions.explanation: The senior signal is naming listing and statistics granularity, not just 'more file opens', and noting the too-big failure mode as well.

questions.prompt: Which three distinct things are all called 'partitioning' in Spark?
options: Input, intermediate and output partitioning
Static, dynamic and adaptive partitioning
Hash, range and round-robin partitioning
Storage partitioning (directories on disk), Spark execution partitions (read parallelism), and shuffle partitions (produced by an Exchange)
questions.explanation: They are unrelated and have separate toolkits. Storage partitioning controls WHAT YOU READ and is set at write time. Execution partitions control HOW MANY TASKS READ IT and are derived from file sizes and maxPartitionBytes. Shuffle partitions control PARALLELISM AFTER A SHUFFLE. 'Increase partitions' is meaningless until you say which — raising shuffle partitions does nothing for a full scan caused by a broken partition filter.

questions.prompt: Adding `.coalesce(10)` before a write took a job from 8 minutes to 90. Why?
options: coalesce avoids a shuffle, so it cannot create a stage boundary — the reduced parallelism propagates backward through the whole preceding stage
coalesce forces a sort before writing
The write commit protocol serialises across partitions
Ten partitions cannot hold the output volume
questions.explanation: The intent was 'compute normally, then merge into 10 files'. What happens is that the entire chain of narrow dependencies in that stage now runs 10-way. The tell is a final stage with exactly 10 very long tasks. If you also multiplied the data each task holds by two hundred, you may now be spilling as well. To merge only at the end you need a shuffle boundary: repartition(10), or a REBALANCE hint.

questions.prompt: What does the `REBALANCE` hint provide that `repartition(n)` does not?
options: It avoids a shuffle entirely
It lets AQE choose partition boundaries to hit an even target size, including splitting skewed ones, instead of you guessing n
It guarantees exactly one output file per storage partition
It preserves the existing sort order
questions.explanation: REBALANCE (available from Spark 3.3) expresses intent as a SIZE target rather than a count, which is the same shift AQE made for shuffle partitions generally. It needs AQE enabled. repartition(n) is still the right tool when you genuinely need a specific number of partitions.

questions.prompt: Why does `repartition(n, col)` NOT fix skew on `col`?
options: AQE immediately re-coalesces the partitions
It uses round-robin distribution, ignoring the column
Hash partitioning by design sends all rows with the same key to one partition
It only applies to RDDs
questions.explanation: Co-locating equal keys is the POINT of hash partitioning — it is what makes joins and aggregations correct. It cannot also spread a single hot value. Repartitioning helps when the current partitioning is bad for an unrelated reason, or when you repartition on a different, better-distributed column.

questions.prompt: When is `repartitionByRange` preferable to `repartition`?
options: When the data is already sorted
When you want to avoid a shuffle
When you need exactly n equally sized partitions
When you want range-partitioned output — useful for sorted writes and range pruning — accepting that boundaries come from sampling
questions.explanation: Range partitioning groups by value ranges rather than hash, which suits sorted output and downstream range filters. The trade-off is that boundaries are chosen by SAMPLING, so partition sizes are approximate and mildly non-deterministic — worth knowing before you rely on exact sizing.

questions.prompt: A query filters on the partition column but input bytes equal the whole table. What do you check?
options: The scan node's PartitionFilters — a function around the column or a type mismatch can prevent or weaken pruning
Whether the shuffle partition count is too low
Whether AQE coalescing merged the read partitions
Whether statistics are up to date
questions.explanation: Wrapping the partition column in a function, or comparing it against a different type so the engine casts the COLUMN, can stop the predicate being used to choose directories. Whether a given expression defeats pruning depends on the expression, the source and the version — so verify against PartitionFilters and the partitions-read metric rather than assuming. Compute the constant side and leave the column bare.

questions.prompt: Which are true of storage partition keys? (Select all that apply.)
options: They should be columns queries actually filter on
High cardinality keys can create unmanageable numbers of directories
Changing them requires rewriting the table
Hour-level partitioning is right when each hour holds substantial data
More partition columns always improves pruning
questions.explanation: The claim that more partition columns always improves pruning is false, and it is the trap: partitioning by an additional high-cardinality column multiplies directory count and makes listing dominate every query, while pruning gains nothing if queries do not filter on it. Modern table formats offer hidden partitioning and transforms that decouple physical layout from literal column values, which usually beats hand-rolled directory schemes where available.

questions.prompt: Distinguish storage partitioning, execution partitions and shuffle partitions, and give a symptom that belongs to each.
questions.model_answer: Storage partitioning is the physical directory layout, set at write time with PARTITIONED BY. It controls WHAT YOU READ. Its symptom is a scan whose input bytes equal the whole table when the query filters on one day — pruning was lost, usually because the partition column was wrapped in a function or compared against a mismatched type, and you confirm it by an empty PartitionFilters in the scan node. Its other failure is high-cardinality keys producing millions of directories, whose symptom is minutes of listing before the first task runs. Execution partitions are the units of read parallelism, derived from file sizes and spark.sql.files.maxPartitionBytes (Apache default 128 MB) plus the small-file packing governed by openCostInBytes. They control HOW MANY TASKS READ IT. Their symptom is thousands of tasks each doing milliseconds of work on a tiny-file table, or too few tasks leaving slots idle. You do not set this directly — you change file layout or the byte thresholds. Shuffle partitions are what an Exchange produces, governed by spark.sql.shuffle.partitions (Apache default 200) as an initial count, then coalesced by AQE toward the advisory size. They control PARALLELISM AFTER A SHUFFLE. Their symptom is disk spill when partitions exceed per-task execution memory, or tiny tasks and tiny output files when there are too many. The practical value of keeping these separate is that 'increase partitions' is meaningless until you say which one — raising shuffle partitions does nothing at all for a full-table scan caused by a broken partition filter.
questions.explanation: The senior signal is one concrete symptom per layer and the observation that the generic advice is unactionable without naming the layer.

questions.prompt: An engineer adds `.cache()` and the job gets 30% SLOWER. Which explanation is most complete?
options: Caching always adds a write step, so some slowdown is expected
Storage and execution share one memory pool, so execution may now spill; cached blocks are long-lived so GC rises; and if it does not fit, evicted blocks are recomputed anyway
The cache was placed after the action instead of before it
Cached data cannot be read by more than one executor
questions.explanation: All three costs can exceed the benefit. Check the Storage tab for the fraction actually cached and the size in memory, check whether spill appeared where there was none, and check GC time. Then ask the diagnostic question FIRST: is this dataset read more than once at all? A cache on a dataset used once is pure loss, and that is the most common version of this bug.

questions.prompt: What is the first question to ask before caching a DataFrame?
options: Has it been repartitioned?
Does it fit in memory?
Is it read more than once?
Is the storage level serialized?
questions.explanation: Reuse is the precondition for any benefit at all. Only then does it matter whether recomputation is expensive, whether it fits, and whether that memory would serve execution better. Most production caches fail at question one.

questions.prompt: Why is caching a dataset far larger than available storage memory the WORST case?
options: The cache silently switches to disk-only and becomes slower than the source
Cached blocks are replicated, doubling the footprint
Spark raises an error and fails the job
Evicted blocks are recomputed on access, so you pay the recomputation you were avoiding PLUS the memory pressure and GC you added
questions.explanation: You get the worst of both worlds. The Storage tab showing 'fraction cached' below 100% is the direct evidence. Meanwhile execution has less memory (possibly introducing spill) and the old generation is full of long-lived objects the collector must scan.

questions.prompt: How does `df.cache()` differ from `CACHE TABLE t` in SQL?
options: df.cache() is lazy — nothing is cached until an action runs — whereas CACHE TABLE is eager by default
CACHE TABLE replicates blocks across executors
df.cache() only caches the schema
They use different storage levels by default
questions.explanation: A useful difference to know when reasoning about when the cost is actually paid. Both are released with unpersist/UNCACHE — the step everyone forgets. In a long-lived session, forgotten caches accumulate silently and are a classic cause of a mysteriously degrading cluster.

questions.prompt: When does caching genuinely earn its keep, and what should you do before caching?
questions.model_answer: It earns its keep when an expensive intermediate is reused several times — a heavy join or aggregation feeding three downstream branches; in iterative algorithms that walk the same dataset repeatedly; when breaking a long lineage before an action that would otherwise recompute a deep chain on retry; and in interactive exploration where a human will query the same intermediate ten times. Before caching, PROJECT and FILTER first: cache the narrow, filtered result you will actually use, not the wide source. Caching 60 columns to read 6 wastes memory by roughly an order of magnitude, and since storage and execution share one pool that waste comes directly out of the memory joins and aggregations need. I would also choose the storage level deliberately — a serialized level cuts memory and GC pressure at the cost of CPU on read, and a disk-inclusive level avoids the recompute-on-eviction trap. Then measure: runtime, spill and GC before and after, because caching is an intervention with a cost and belongs in the same one-variable experimental loop as any config change. And always pair it with an unpersist at the end of the dataset's useful life.
questions.explanation: The senior signal is 'project before you cache' plus treating caching as a measured intervention rather than a free speedup.

questions.prompt: You double the executor count and runtime improves by 8%. What does that tell you?
options: The job needs even more executors
The job is not limited by available slots — and you just roughly doubled the cost for 8%
Dynamic allocation is misconfigured
The shuffle partition count should be doubled to match
questions.explanation: Candidates: a single stage whose wall clock is set by one enormous task, so extra slots have nothing to do; a serial phase (listing, plan compilation, write commit) that does not parallelise; a throughput limit on the storage side; or the driver being the constraint, in which case more executors actively hurt. Confirm via slot utilisation over time — if many slots are idle during the slow stage, capacity was never the problem.

questions.prompt: Why is `spark.executor.cores` described as a memory decision disguised as a CPU decision?
options: Because Spark allocates one JVM per core
Because each core reserves a fixed amount of heap
Because unified memory is per executor and shared by concurrent tasks, so per-task memory is roughly (heap x memory.fraction) / cores
Because cores determine the number of shuffle partitions
questions.explanation: Halving cores doubles per-task memory without buying a gigabyte — which is why 'reduce executor cores' recurs in the OOM fix list, and why very fat executors reliably spill. In PySpark it matters twice over, because there is one Python worker process per concurrent task. The counter-pressure is more JVMs for the same capacity, each with its own overhead and its own copy of every broadcast.

questions.prompt: What is the Apache default for `spark.dynamicAllocation.enabled`?
options: true only on YARN
It depends on spark.master
true
false
questions.explanation: False in Apache Spark, though managed platforms frequently enable it. This is a good example of why the Environment tab outranks documentation: a 'Spark default' quoted from a vendor blog is a vendor default.

questions.prompt: Why does dynamic allocation need shuffle tracking or an external shuffle service?
options: Because an executor holding shuffle output another stage still needs cannot simply be released without forcing re-execution
To allow executors to be added mid-stage
To keep broadcast variables alive across stages
To let executors share cached blocks
questions.explanation: Shuffle output lives on the producing executor's local disk and is not replicated. Releasing such an executor destroys map output and forces the map stage to re-run — exactly the fetch-failure cascade. `spark.dynamicAllocation.shuffleTracking.enabled` (Apache default false) makes Spark keep executors that still hold needed shuffle data; an external shuffle service solves it by decoupling the data from executor lifetime.

questions.prompt: A cluster is sized for its widest stage but sits at 7% slot utilisation through a long final tail. What is the right response?
options: Lower spark.dynamicAllocation.executorIdleTimeout and accept the tail
Fix the tail's distribution — the skew or imbalance that makes two tasks hold the whole cluster
Increase maxExecutors so the tail finishes sooner
Enable speculative execution
questions.explanation: Lowering the idle timeout treats the cost symptom, and can help, but the tail itself is the defect: the cluster is fully billed while doing almost nothing. Increasing maxExecutors is the classic false win — it buys parallelism for the wide middle stage and pays for all of it through a tail only two tasks are using.

questions.prompt: Which are genuine costs of running many small executors (one or two cores each)? (Select all that apply.)
options: More JVMs to start and manage
Every broadcast variable is copied into each executor
More shuffle connections between executors
Less opportunity for tasks to share work within an executor
Less memory available per task
questions.explanation: More JVMs, a broadcast copy per executor, more shuffle connections and less in-executor sharing are all real overheads of going too narrow. Memory per task is the one that IMPROVES as cores per executor fall, since unified memory is divided among concurrent tasks — that is precisely the trade-off. There is a middle band, it is workload-dependent, and it is found by experiment rather than by a number from a conference talk.

questions.prompt: Explain why 'more executors' is not a general answer to a slow Spark job.
questions.model_answer: Adding executors makes a job WIDER, and width only helps if there is work waiting for a slot. Several common situations have no such work. If one stage's wall clock is set by a single enormous task — skew — then 4,999 slots are already idle and adding more changes nothing while multiplying the bill. If part of the job is serial (driver-side file listing, plan compilation, the write commit) that portion does not scale at all, so Amdahl's law caps the gain. If the constraint is the DRIVER — millions of tasks to schedule and track, or thousands of tiny jobs from a loop — then more executors make it strictly worse, because the same single coordinator now has more to do. If the constraint is storage throughput or per-prefix throttling, more executors means more clients contending on the same throttled path. Meanwhile cost scales almost exactly linearly with executor-hours, so a change that improves runtime 8% while doubling capacity is a 92% cost increase reported as a win. The honest framing is not 'can we make it faster' but 'what is the cheapest configuration that meets the SLA' — a job finishing at 04:10 against an 06:00 deadline gains nothing from finishing at 03:50. The diagnostic that settles it in a minute is slot utilisation over time: if allocated executors greatly exceed active tasks during the slow stage, capacity was never the bottleneck.
questions.explanation: The senior signal is naming the specific non-scaling components and reporting executor-hours alongside runtime.

questions.prompt: What is the Apache default for `spark.speculation`?
options: It is determined by the cluster manager
true
false
true when dynamic allocation is enabled
questions.explanation: False in Apache Spark, though many managed platforms enable it. Related defaults: spark.speculation.multiplier 1.5 (how much slower than the comparison a task must be) and spark.speculation.quantile 0.75 (the fraction of tasks that must complete before speculation may start).

questions.prompt: Why does speculative execution NOT cure data skew?
options: It is disabled automatically when AQE skew handling is on
It requires deterministic tasks, which skewed joins are not
It only applies to the first attempt of each task
It duplicates the same pathological partition onto another executor, where it takes just as long, while consuming a slot
questions.explanation: Speculation is a hedge against a slow HOST. Against skew you add cost and remove capacity for zero benefit, because the duplicate must process the same enormous partition. It also has a correctness dimension: for non-idempotent work — writing to an external system, calling an API, incrementing a counter — running a task twice may do the thing twice.

questions.prompt: Slow tasks are concentrated on one executor id across multiple different stages. What does that indicate?
options: An unhealthy host or noisy neighbour — the fix is to drain it, not to tune Spark
The executor has too little memory allocated
AQE is assigning it larger partitions
Data skew on a shared key
questions.explanation: Grouping the slowest tasks by executor and host takes thirty seconds and is conclusive when the same host recurs across unrelated stages. Skew would follow the DATA, appearing wherever the hot key lands rather than tracking one machine. Check that executor's GC ratio and the host's disk I/O wait to confirm.

questions.prompt: A single task runs 12 minutes while 100 peers finish in 30 seconds. Diagnose it.
questions.model_answer: The discriminator is one column: the slow task's input or shuffle-read bytes versus the median. If it read on the order of a hundred times more, duration scales with work and this is skew — I go find the hot key with a GROUP BY and percentage-of-total, checking specifically for sentinels like -1 or 'UNKNOWN' and for NULL, and remediate by filtering keys that cannot match, isolating hot keys into a broadcast branch, or salting an additive aggregation. If instead it read a NORMAL amount and simply took longer, duration does not scale with data and the cause is environmental: I check whether it and other slow tasks share an executor or host, then that executor's GC time as a fraction of run time, then the host's CPU and disk I/O wait — a degraded local volume or a noisy co-tenant produces exactly this pattern. Speculative execution is the right hedge for the second case and useless for the first, which is a compact way to state the difference. It is worth being explicit about the economics either way: 100 slots sat idle for 11.5 minutes while being fully billed, so a straggler is a cost problem even when the job succeeds. If the same host recurs across multiple stages or multiple days, the fix is to drain and replace it rather than to tune Spark at all.
questions.explanation: The senior signal is refusing to call it skew before checking input size, and naming speculation as the fix for exactly one of the two branches.

questions.prompt: What is the Apache default for `spark.network.timeout`?
questions.explanation: 120s. It is the default timeout for most network interactions including heartbeat-based failure detection. Raising it is the classic 'larger waiting room' fix — the patient waits longer without getting better. It is occasionally justified on a genuinely high-latency network or during a known long pause you are actively working to remove, but never as step one.

questions.prompt: Why is raising `spark.shuffle.io.maxRetries` a poor first response to fetch failures?
options: It conflicts with speculative execution
Retries are not supported for remote blocks
If the executor holding the blocks is dead the data is gone, so more retries add waiting rather than success — and each retry delays discovering the real cause
It increases the shuffle partition count implicitly
questions.explanation: Retries only help when the block is still there and the failure was transient. Since shuffle output dies with its executor, the first question is always whether an executor died — check the Executors tab for removals near the failure timestamp and read that executor's own log. Retry settings are a resilience knob for genuinely transient conditions, not a diagnosis.

questions.prompt: Describe the spill feedback loop that turns a memory problem into an executor-loss cascade.
options: Spill increases shuffle partitions, which increases scheduling overhead
Spill forces recomputation of cached blocks, which increases memory pressure
Spill causes GC, which causes more spill
Memory pressure causes spill, spill saturates local disk I/O, tasks slow, executors live longer accumulating more shuffle files, disk fills, executors die and their map output is lost
questions.explanation: It is self-reinforcing, which is why it must be broken at the TOP. Provisioning bigger or faster local disks buys time; only reducing memory pressure — smaller partitions, fewer cores per executor, removing an unnecessary shuffle — ends it.

questions.prompt: Which symptom set points at local disk rather than memory or network?
options: Rising disk spill, task times creeping up as the stage progresses, and executor loss with 'No space left on device'
High shuffle read blocked time across all tasks
Long gaps between stages with no active stage
High GC with uniform task durations
questions.explanation: Spark needs local scratch for BOTH shuffle files and spill, and it is invisible in most monitoring. Check host disk utilisation and I/O wait on the SCRATCH volume specifically — often a different device from the root volume — and check how many local dirs are configured, since spreading scratch across multiple physical devices raises aggregate throughput.

questions.prompt: Which are plausible causes of a `FetchFailedException`? (Select all that apply.)
options: The executor holding the shuffle blocks died
Local disk failure or a full scratch volume where shuffle files were written
Genuine network problems such as saturation or a security-group change
Individual shuffle blocks so large that transfers time out
The query used the wrong join strategy
questions.explanation: A dead executor, a failed or full scratch volume, genuine network problems and oversized shuffle blocks are all real mechanisms. Join strategy is not a direct cause — though a bad strategy can produce enormous shuffle volume, which fills disks and creates oversized blocks, which then produces fetch failures. That is a cascade, and distinguishing the origin from the symptom is exactly the point.

questions.prompt: Executor losses were 'fixed' three months ago by raising the network timeout to 600s. Runtime has crept up 40% since. What most likely happened?
options: The longer timeout increased scheduling overhead
A degraded host stopped being evicted, so Spark keeps scheduling work onto a machine that cannot do it
Dynamic allocation stopped releasing idle executors
The larger timeout increased shuffle buffer sizes
questions.explanation: Raising the timeout stopped Spark declaring the unhealthy executor dead. Instead of losing it quickly, the job keeps assigning tasks to it. The evidence is slow tasks concentrated on one executor across multiple stages and days, with ORDINARY input sizes — and host metrics showing disk I/O wait far above its peers. The fix is draining the host and restoring the timeout, not tuning around it.

questions.prompt: A query adds `DISTINCT` to remove duplicates that appeared after a join. What is the deeper problem?
options: DISTINCT forces a broadcast join
DISTINCT is slower than GROUP BY
DISTINCT is usually a bandage over a cardinality bug — the join fanned out, and a semi-join expresses the real intent without multiplying rows
DISTINCT prevents predicate pushdown
questions.explanation: DISTINCT forces a full shuffle and aggregation over every selected column, and it hides the fact that the join produced rows it should not have. If the intent is 'orders that have items', EXISTS or a semi-join never fans out in the first place. Fixing the cardinality is both faster and more correct.

questions.prompt: Why is a global `ORDER BY` on 4 billion rows expensive, and what is usually intended instead?
options: It disables AQE for the whole query
It prevents column pruning
It forces a broadcast; use a hint instead
A total order needs range-partitioning plus a sort and can serialise at the end; usually people want either ORDER BY with LIMIT, or SORT BY within partitions for sorted files
questions.explanation: ORDER BY with LIMIT is a different physical operation — the engine can keep only the top N per partition, shown as TakeOrderedAndProject. And 'the output files should be sorted' is SORT BY within partitions, which is cheap, not ORDER BY, which is not.

questions.prompt: Three subqueries each count a different event type from the same partition. What is the better pattern?
options: One scan with conditional aggregation — COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE ...) per type
Union the three results
Repartition by event type first
Cache the table before the subqueries
questions.explanation: Three subqueries are three scans of the same data. Conditional aggregation reads it once. The same principle applies to CTEs referenced multiple times — a CTE is not automatically materialised, so referencing it three times can mean computing it three times unless the optimizer reuses the exchange. Count Scan nodes in the plan and look for ReusedExchange.

questions.prompt: Why is an unbounded `explode()` a distinctive kind of skew risk?
options: It always produces a cartesian product
It multiplies rows AFTER the shuffle boundary, so skew it creates cannot be addressed by AQE's shuffle-partition splitting
It disables whole-stage code generation
It forces a sort on the exploded column
questions.explanation: Array-length distributions are almost always heavy-tailed — one crawler session with hundreds of thousands of page views becomes one enormous partition. AQE reasons about shuffle partitions; skew generated downstream of that boundary is outside what it can split. Check the Generate node's output rows against its input rows, profile array-length percentiles, and bound or filter before exploding.

questions.prompt: Input rows are flat but output rows rose 410% overnight with no code change. What is the FIRST hypothesis?
options: Statistics went stale and changed the join strategy
Traffic spiked and the cluster needs resizing
A join fanned out — most likely duplicate keys in a dimension or a dropped current-record filter
The shuffle partition count is now too low
questions.explanation: Flat input with multiplied output is a cardinality event, and a near-round multiple is the tell — organic growth is not a round multiple. Test with GROUP BY key HAVING COUNT(*) > 1 on each dimension. Remember it is simultaneously a correctness incident: every downstream aggregate has been inflated since it started.

questions.prompt: A pipeline unchanged for a year suddenly takes 4 hours instead of 40 minutes. No deploy, no config change. What are the first three checks?
options: GC time, spill, and task count
The physical plan, the Storage tab, and the event log
Executor count, memory settings, and shuffle partitions
Input bytes and rows versus the same weekday; output-over-input row ratio; input file count and bytes-per-file
questions.explanation: With nothing changed on your side, the change is in the DATA or the environment. A source that reprocessed history or a duplicate load explains everything instantly and is not a Spark problem. A moved output-per-input ratio means a fan-out — and a correctness incident. A jump in file count with flat bytes means an upstream writer changed. Only if all three are flat do you diff the physical plan against a previous run.

questions.prompt: Which data-quality events commonly present as Spark performance incidents? (Select all that apply.)
options: Duplicate dimension rows
A surge in NULLs on a join key
Record-size explosion with flat row counts
An upstream writer switching to micro-batches, multiplying file count
A change to spark.sql.shuffle.partitions
questions.explanation: Duplicate dimension rows, a NULL surge, record-size explosion and a file-count jump are all data or layout events that surface as slowness, which is why input/output volume counters belong on the dashboard before any Spark-side metric. The last is a configuration change — a real cause of slowness, but not a data-quality event, and it would show up in the Environment tab rather than in volume counters.

questions.prompt: Give three SQL changes that speed up a slow Spark query and say how you would PROVE each one worked.
questions.model_answer: I would order them by which cost they cut and name the confirming metric for each. First, cut bytes SCANNED: project explicit columns instead of SELECT *, and keep the partition predicate on a bare, correctly-typed column so directory pruning applies. Proof is the scan node — ReadSchema listing only the needed columns, PartitionFilters populated, the partitions-read metric matching expectation, and input bytes dropping from table size to partition size. Second, cut bytes SHUFFLED: pre-aggregate before the join so you move eight million pre-aggregated rows rather than four billion raw ones, or restore a broadcast that stale statistics turned into a sort-merge join. Proof is shuffle write bytes for that stage falling, and the join node in the SQL tab of the finished run changing strategy — the finished run, because AQE can re-plan and a static EXPLAIN is only a proposal. Third, cut bytes WRITTEN and re-read: make the job incremental so it touches one partition instead of recomputing history, and collapse repeated scans of the same source into one pass with conditional aggregation. Proof is output bytes, output file count, and the number of Scan nodes in the plan. In every case I capture the before numbers first and change one thing at a time, because the failure mode in this work is making three changes and being unable to attribute the improvement to any of them — and I would record executor-hours alongside runtime, since a change that improves wall clock while increasing total work is a trade-off to be argued rather than a win to be announced.
questions.explanation: The senior signal is naming a confirming metric per change and insisting on the finished-run plan rather than EXPLAIN.

questions.prompt: Version A: 90 min on 100 executors (150 executor-hours). Version B: 50 min on 500 executors (417 executor-hours). The SLA is 06:00 and both finish comfortably. Which is better?
options: A — it meets the SLA at roughly 36% of the cost, and the 40 minutes B buys are worth nothing against that deadline
B, because faster jobs free the cluster for other work
They are equivalent since both meet the SLA
B — it is 44% faster
questions.explanation: Runtime is the metric everyone optimises because it is visible; cost is the one the business feels. When headroom against the SLA is already comfortable, extra speed has no consumer. The interesting middle option in practice is usually a version like 58 min on 180 executors — 92% of B's speed at ~42% of B's cost — because the curve flattens as the serial and skewed portions stop scaling.

questions.prompt: Which metric best reveals that a 'performance win' actually bought speed with money?
options: Total shuffle bytes
Executor-hours — if it rises while runtime falls, you scaled capacity rather than removing work
Task count
Peak executor memory
questions.explanation: Executor-hours is the cost proxy that stays honest. The version worth being proud of is the one where runtime improved AND executor-hours fell, because that means you removed work — usually a plan or layout fix — rather than buying parallelism. Reporting both together is what stops a 40% speedup that tripled the bill from being announced as a win.

questions.prompt: Why is 'cost per TB processed' a useful metric to trend?
options: It identifies which team owns each pipeline
It is required for chargeback accounting
It normalises for data growth, so it should FALL over time as layout, pruning and join strategy improve
It correlates directly with runtime
questions.explanation: If data volume grew 3x and cost grew 3x, nothing improved — that is linear scaling, the baseline rather than an achievement. Cost per TB keeps improving when you make the job cheaper, not just faster, which is the behaviour worth rewarding.

questions.prompt: Which cost source is entirely invisible in the Spark UI?
options: Executor idle time during a long tail
Re-executed stages after fetch failures
Shuffle volume
Cluster startup and provisioning time
questions.explanation: Cluster creation happens before the application exists, so only the orchestrator's timestamps reveal it — and on short pipelines it can be a substantial share of the bill. Shuffle volume, idle capacity and re-execution are all visible inside Spark itself — in stage metrics, in slot utilisation over time, and in stage attempt counts respectively.

questions.prompt: Which changes reduce cost WITHOUT necessarily reducing runtime? (Select all that apply.)
options: Fixing a skewed tail so the cluster can be sized smaller
Removing re-execution caused by executor loss
Eliminating a repeated scan of the same source
Shrinking the cluster to use up genuine SLA headroom
Raising spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold globally
questions.explanation: Fixing the tail, removing re-execution, eliminating a repeated scan and using up genuine SLA headroom all remove wasted work or wasted capacity. Raising the broadcast threshold globally is a risk transfer, not a saving: it increases driver memory pressure for every join in every query, and if the estimate was wrong to begin with it amplifies the error. Note that a job finishing three hours before its deadline has headroom that is currently being spent on nothing.

questions.prompt: How would you reduce a pipeline's cost by 40% without breaking its SLA?
questions.model_answer: I would separate cost into work I can DELETE and capacity I can stop BUYING, and attack the first because it improves both axes at once. Work I can delete: bytes scanned — restore partition pruning, project only needed columns, and collapse repeated scans of the same source into one pass; bytes shuffled — broadcast what should broadcast (usually by fixing statistics rather than adding hints), pre-aggregate before joins, and remove defensive repartitions that exist 'to be safe'; bytes written — make the job incremental rather than recomputing history; and re-executed work, since any stage attempt above one has been paid for twice, which usually traces back to a single executor death worth root-causing. Capacity I can stop buying: I look at slot utilisation over time, because most clusters are sized for their widest stage and then idle through a long tail, so fixing the tail's skew often lets me cut the cluster substantially with almost no runtime change; I check instance shape against actual use, since a memory-shaped instance for a CPU-bound job wastes half of what it costs; and on short pipelines I check provisioning time, which is invisible in the Spark UI and can be a third of the bill. Then I check whether the SLA is real by asking the consumer when they actually need the data — a job finishing at 03:00 against an 06:00 deadline has three hours of headroom being spent on nothing. I would report the result as executor-hours and cost per TB rather than runtime, because those are the numbers that stay honest as data grows.
questions.explanation: The senior signal is the delete-work-before-buying-less-capacity ordering, and treating the SLA itself as something to verify rather than assume.
